title: [Feat] Observe elastic EP scaling state in PodAutoscaler status
body:
### Pull Request Description

Issue #2288 asks the autoscaler to drive elastic expert parallelism for MoE serving, and asks to start observe-only before acting on it. This PR is that first step on the read side. The custom autoscaling path records the observed engine scaling state in the PodAutoscaler status and changes no replica decision.

The engine answers `POST /is_scaling_elastic_ep` with a boolean. While a scaling commit is in flight the engine answers every HTTP request with a 503 whose body says the model is currently scaling, so the probe maps that response to scaling as well. The DP coordinator wave state stays inside the engine process and has no HTTP surface today, so this step observes the endpoint only.

On each reconcile of the custom autoscaling path used by KPA and APA, the controller:

- selects the engine pods of the scale target that are ready, have an IP, and enable elastic EP on the command line through `--enable-elastic-ep` or `--elastic-ep-max-dp-size`
- resolves the engine ports the way the gateway does, the `model.aibrix.ai/port` label with the data parallel size first, then `--port`, `VLLM_PORT`, and the declared container ports
- probes the endpoint with a 2 second timeout per probe, at most 8 probes in flight, and a 3 second budget for the whole observation
- records the aggregate in `status.elasticEPScaling`, which carries `inProgress`, `observedEngines`, `scalingEngines`, and `lastTransitionTime`

The deliberate choices worth reviewing:

- An engine that does not answer is not counted. When no engine reports a state, the observation returns nothing and the previous status is kept, so a timeout never reads as not scaling.
- `lastTransitionTime` moves only when `inProgress` changes, so a steady state does not rewrite the status on every reconcile.
- Pods that do not enable elastic EP are never probed, so the observation adds no traffic for targets that do not use it.
- Enablement through a vLLM config file is not detected, only the command line flags.
- The HPA path is untouched and no scaling behavior depends on the new field yet. Acting on the state is the next step of #2288.

### Review Guide

The change is 1171 added lines across 11 files. The two new files are most of it. Reading order:

1. `api/autoscaling/v1alpha1/podautoscaler_types.go` +30: the new `ElasticEPScalingStatus` type and the new status field.
2. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/elastic_ep.go` new, 375: `probe` owns the response semantics, `elasticEPEngineContainer` and `elasticEPEnginePorts` own engine selection, `observeElasticEPScaling` owns the aggregation and the concurrency bound, and `mergeElasticEPScalingStatus` owns the transition time.
3. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/podautoscaler_controller.go` +81/-33: the wiring. Step 6 of `reconcileCustomPA` observes before the single status update, the three status constructors carry the field, and the pod listing that `computeMetricBasedReplicas` already did moves into `getPodsForScale` so both callers share it. The extraction keeps the existing selector behavior, including the RayClusterFleet head filter.
4. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/elastic_ep_test.go` new, 561: the probe semantics matrix, the port resolution table, the aggregation over a fake client with live test servers, the timestamp semantics, and the status carry-over.
5. Generated files: the deepcopy, the two CRD copies, and the apply configuration.

Worth checking closely: the 503 mapping accepts the marker only in that status code, the aggregation does not count unreachable engines, and the observation cannot extend a reconcile beyond its 3 second budget.

### Test Plan

- `go test ./pkg/controller/podautoscaler/... -count=1` passes.
- The new tests pass under `-race`, and the prober matrix passes over repeated runs.
- `golangci-lint` v2.13.1 reports 0 issues for the whole repository.
- `hack/verify-codegen.sh`, `make manifests`, and `hack/verify-crd-sync.sh` pass with no diff, the same sequence the CI verify job runs.
- `go build ./...` and `go vet` pass.
- The new file reports 92 percent statement coverage for the probe, 95 for the observation, and 100 for engine selection and the merge.

title: [Feat] Support predictive autoscaling in the PodAutoscaler
body:
### Pull Request Description

> **Draft.** The API shape is being settled in #1418, where the proposal is posted. The commits are ordered API first, then the projection, then the wiring, with the zero-replica fix folded into the wiring commit. Integration and E2E tests follow as the last commits. This PR stays in draft and follows whatever is agreed in #1418.

#1418 asks for predictive autoscaling for LLM inference, where a pod start-up takes long
enough that reacting to a metric spike is always late. This change adds an opt-in
`spec.predictive` block to the `PodAutoscaler`. The controller projects the metric trend of
the observation window forward, records the projection in `status.predictive`, and, in `Auto`
mode, uses it as a floor for scale-up. The reactive path keeps its role: the projection can
raise a decision, never lower one, and the default mode changes nothing.

The claim comment on the issue mentioned sending this as separate PRs. It ships as one
because the three pieces are one API surface: piece 1 alone would merge `spec.predictive`
and `status.predictive` with nothing that writes the status, and the predictor has no caller
until the decision pipeline composes it. With `Preview` as the default mode, merging it
whole still ships no behaviour change until a workload opts into `Auto`, which is the
property the separate pieces were meant to protect.

On the two open questions from the claim comment: the projection lives in a `predictive`
sub-block rather than in `metricsSources`, because it composes with the sources instead of
replacing one; and the up/down philosophy is a safety floor rather than confidence
blending, so the reactive algorithm keeps deciding when capacity is released.

### Semantics

- **Preview first.** `mode` defaults to `Preview`, where the controller computes the
  projection and writes it to `status.predictive`, and the replica decision stays exactly as
  it is without the block. `Auto` turns the projection into a floor:
  `final = max(reactive, projected)`.
- **Up only.** The projection never triggers or lowers a scale-down, so reactive scaling
  keeps full control of releasing capacity. The floor is capped by the configured scale-up
  rate, and the result still passes through `minReplicas`, `maxReplicas`, the active
  `schedules` entry and the scale-up cooldown window.
- **An honest baseline.** The projection is a least-squares line over the samples inside
  `observeWindowSeconds`, evaluated at `horizonSeconds` (2 minutes when unset). It is
  clamped at zero and at four times the observed mean, and it is only produced from at least
  three samples spanning at least half of the window, so a fresh `PodAutoscaler` reports
  nothing until the history supports it.
- **Same formula as the reactive path.** A projected value becomes replicas with the formula
  of the active strategy, `ceil(value / targetValue)` for KPA and
  `ceil(currentReplicas * value / targetValue)` for APA, so the two numbers `Auto` compares
  are the same kind of number.
- **HPA is out of scope.** The HPA strategy delegates its decision to a native
  `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` resource, which has no channel to receive a projection, so the
  validating webhook rejects the combination instead of accepting a block that would do
  nothing.
- **No spec churn when it is off.** Without `spec.predictive` nothing is projected and
  `status.predictive` stays absent; removing the block clears it.

### Review guide

The diff is large because the API, the projection, the wiring, the generated artifacts and the tests land together. The three commits follow the same order as the list below. Reading order:

1. `api/autoscaling/v1alpha1/podautoscaler_types.go` (+63) - the whole API surface: `PredictiveSpec` (`mode`, `horizonSeconds`) and `PredictiveStatus` (`mode`, `observedValue`, `predictedValue`, `predictedReplicas`, `lastUpdated`). The status values are strings, matching how metric values are compared elsewhere in the API and keeping a float diff out of the status.
2. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/prediction/predictor.go` (new, 201) with `predictor_test.go` - the projection: `Project` windows the samples and projects a least-squares line `horizon` forward, `leastSquares` is the fit, and the constants at the top of the file are the guards (minimum samples, minimum coverage, the clamp at zero, the growth cap).
3. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/autoscaler.go` (+160) - where the projection joins the decision. `applyPredictiveFloor` is the merge (`max(reactive, projected)`), `evaluatePrediction` picks the projection that asks for the most replicas, and `predictedReplicas` converts a value with the formula of the active strategy. `ComputeDesiredReplicas` gains one call after the pending-replica guard; the reactive algorithms themselves are not modified.
4. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/podautoscaler_controller.go` (+55/-3) - the only edited lines in the PR: the `setStatus` signature and its three call sites now carry the evaluation, and `predictiveStatus`, `keepPredictiveObservationTime` and `formatMetricValue` write it. `lastUpdated` only moves when the projection changes, so a steady series does not rewrite the status on every resync.
5. `pkg/webhook/podautoscaler_webhook.go` (+35) with `podautoscaler_predictive_test.go` - `validatePredictive`: the mode enum, the horizon range and the HPA rejection.
6. `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/types/metrics.go` and `metrics/client.go` (+25 together) - the two accessors (`Snapshot`, `GetMetricSeries`) that hand the recorded series to the fit. The window statistics keep feeding the reactive algorithms unchanged.

Everything else is mechanical or documentation, safe to skim: `zz_generated.deepcopy.go`, both `autoscaling.aibrix.ai_podautoscalers.yaml` copies and the five `pkg/client/applyconfiguration` files are produced by `make manifests` and `hack/update-codegen.sh`; `docs/source/features/autoscaling/predictive-autoscaling.rst` and `samples/autoscaling/predictive-kpa.yaml` are the fastest way to see the intended user experience. `autoscaler_predictive_test.go` and `predictive_status_test.go` cover the composition and the status in the same order.

What is worth checking closely: (a) without `spec.predictive` nothing is projected and `status.predictive` stays absent, and in `Preview` the replica decision stays with the reactive path, so the "no behaviour change" claim holds; (b) the floor can only raise `DesiredReplicas`, never lower it, and the scale-up rate caps it the same way it caps the reactive recommendations; (c) a projection is only reported once three samples inside the window span at least half of it, and it is clamped at zero and at four times the observed mean; (d) the HPA strategy is rejected instead of silently ignored.

### Test Plan

- `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt -l` and a `-race` run over the podautoscaler and webhook
  packages are clean.
- `hack/verify-codegen.sh` reports `pkg/client` up to date, `make manifests` plus
  `hack/verify-crd-sync.sh` pass, and `sphinx-build -W` builds the docs.
- `prediction/predictor_test.go` covers a projected rise, insufficient samples,
  insufficient window coverage, the clamp at zero, the runaway-growth cap, samples outside
  the window or after the evaluation time, the default horizon and a non-positive window.
- `autoscaler_predictive_test.go` covers `Preview` leaving the decision untouched, `Auto`
  raising it, `Auto` never lowering it, the scale-up rate cap, HPA being skipped, an absent
  block, insufficient history, the KPA and APA replica formulas, and one end-to-end run
  through `ComputeDesiredReplicas`.
- `predictive_status_test.go` covers the status conversion, the stable `lastUpdated` and the
  block being cleared; `podautoscaler_predictive_test.go` covers the accepted modes and the
  rejected HPA, mode and horizon cases.

title: [Feat] Add adaptive bucket serving to the pd prefill routing
body:
### Pull Request Description

BucketServe (arXiv 2507.17120) serves prompts of similar length together so the engine batches are length-homogeneous. A gateway cannot form engine batches, so this PR lands the gateway half of the idea: where several rolesets declare overlapping prompt-length ranges, the gateway splits the overlap into one band per roleset, adapts the cut points to the traffic it observes, and the prefill path prefers the roleset a request length is banded to. Each roleset then receives a length-homogeneous slice of the load, which is what lets the engine-side batches be homogeneous in turn.

The plan is advisory on purpose. `filterPrefillDecodePods` applies it after the load-imbalance fast paths and only while the banded roleset still has both a prefill and a decode candidate; when it does not, or when the plan holds no band for the request's length, the fast paths' choice stands. A stale band therefore costs balance, never correctness.

**Scope**: gateway routing only. No pod, engine, deployment, autoscaling, or CRD change. Off by default (`AIBRIX_BUCKET_SERVE=false`), and with the switch off the routing path is unchanged. The feature requires prompt-length bucketing to be on, because the plan only re-orders the rolesets that bucketing already filtered to.

### How it works

- Per model, the tracker keeps a log2 histogram of the prompt lengths this gateway routes, decayed with a 30s EWMA half-life, and recomputes the plan at most once every 5s or when the roleset set changes.
- The declared ranges are cut into segments whose covering set does not change. Every roleset is first charged the traffic only it can serve, and the remaining cuts are placed so each roleset ends up carrying the model's traffic in proportion to its prefill replica count. A segment shared by two or more rolesets needs 5% of the model's traffic before it is split, and one plan holds at most 16 affinity bands; a wide overlap that cannot afford a band per needing roleset splits into as many bands as the budget left allows, and an interval that is not split keeps every covering roleset a candidate.
- `AIBRIX_BUCKET_SERVE_MODE` picks what the cuts balance: `throughput` (default) places them at prompt-token quantiles, `rps` at request-count quantiles.
- Both the switch and the mode are per profile (`routingConfig.bucketServe` and `routingConfig.bucketServeMode`), so one model can run the plan while another does not.
- The plan is computed outside `selectMu`, the way the policy Prepare step is, and only its application runs under the lock.

```
bucketServeBand()   before selectMu, one call per request
    observe promptLength -> groups -> plan -> band

filterPrefillDecodePods()
    steps 1-5: bucket filter and the load-imbalance fast paths
    banded roleset still has both sides  -> narrow to it
    otherwise                            -> fast paths' choice stands
```

Metrics: `pd_bucket_serve_band_total` and `pd_bucket_serve_prompt_tokens_total` (label `roleset`) count the requests and the prompt tokens each banded roleset carried, so a counter joins the pods that received the band, and the `pd_bucket_serve_band_max` gauge holds the current upper prompt-length bound of the band a roleset holds, deleted when the roleset leaves the plan.

### Review guide

The diff is large because the planner, its specs, the knobs, the metrics, and the docs all land together, but most of it is mechanical. Reading order:

1. `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/bucket_serving.go` (new, 652 lines) - the whole new algorithm. `Band` is the one request-path entry point: it decays and records the traffic picture, recomputes a model's plan when the cached one for its mode and roleset set is stale, and returns the band that covers the length together with the rolesets the new plan dropped. `computeBands`/`bucketServeSegments`/`bucketServeCuts` are the planner.
2. `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd_disaggregation.go` (+146/-11) - the wiring, in three places: `bucketServeMode`, `bucketServeGroups` and `podPromptLenBucketBounds` above `filterPrefillDecodePods`, then `bucketServeBand` and `publishBucketServePlan`, then two blocks inside `filterPrefillDecodePods` (the plan before the lock, the band filter after the fast paths). The band filter is the only routing-behavior change.
3. `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/bucket_serving_test.go` (new, 400) - the planner specs: replica-proportional splitting, exclusive tails, thin intervals kept whole, the band budget, the mode moving the cut, plan caching and refresh, the rolesets that leave a plan, EWMA decay, nil safety, and the environment loader.
4. `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd_bucketing_test.go` (+202/-11) - three routing specs: the band picks the roleset and reports its counter, gauge and label, the band loses to the load-imbalance fast path and is not counted, and the switch off keeps the planner from publishing anything.
5. Everything else is plumbing and docs, all mechanical: `pkg/types/pd_knobs.go` and `pkg/types/routing_config.go` (the two knobs), `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/env_overrides.go` and `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/profile_knobs.go` (loading and validation), `pkg/metrics/gateway_metrics.go` (three metric definitions), `pkg/plugins/gateway/ENV_VARS.md`, `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd_readme.md`, and the two `docs/source/features/` pages.

What is worth checking closely: (a) with the switch off, nothing on the routing path changed; (b) the plan can never remove a candidate the fast paths already chose; (c) no new lock is taken while `selectMu` is held; (d) the label space is the rolesets that hold a band, bounded by the plan cap.

### Test Plan

- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/metrics/... ./pkg/types/...`
- `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/...`
- `golangci-lint run ./pkg/...` reports 0 issues.
- `sphinx-build -b html -W --keep-going docs/source docs/_build/html` builds the docs, the same way the Docs Build workflow does.
- Mutation checks: stubbing the switch check out of `bucketServeBand` turns the switch-off routing spec red, and disabling the band filter in `filterPrefillDecodePods` turns the band-picking routing spec red.

### Related Issues

Refs #1817. This is the gateway-side v1 of the issue. The planner tunables (half-life, refresh interval, minimum split share, band cap) ship as code defaults for now; a configuration knob for them, and any engine or autoscaling follow-up, are out of scope here and can follow in separate PRs.

title: [Bug] Harden tokenizer pool capacity test and unlock before logging
body:
## Pull Request Description

The concurrent capacity test added in #2719 could count a retry from one caller as a second caller: its 1s client timeout expired while the health handler waited at a 5s barrier. A health-check failure could then satisfy the different-model fallback assertion without exercising the locked capacity recheck.

- Use the default 30s client timeout, cancellable handler waits, and bounded waits for both callers. Require zero tokenizer-creation failures so a health-check timeout cannot masquerade as a capacity rejection. Caller completion and the failure counter establish client-side health-check success without a separate response-write signal. Release handlers and join callers before closing the pool.
- Look up the model entry once in the commit section and unlock before logging. Preserve the existing capacity checks and closing of discarded or replaced clients.

The two sequential regression tests and the TTL policy are retained. An entry that expires during a health check does not reserve its old slot; refreshing `lastUsed` for failing attempts would change eviction behavior. No API or configuration changes.

## Related Issues

Follow-up to #2719, following the [maintainer's suggestion](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pull/2719#issuecomment-5824514084), addressing the [further review](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pull/2719#issuecomment-5824381397) and [simplification feedback](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pull/2719#issuecomment-5824381393).

title: [CI] Serialize the poetry install in the Python tests workflow
body:
### Pull Request Description

The Python tests workflow upgrades pip and poetry in place and then runs `poetry install` with the default parallel installer:

```yaml
- name: Install dependencies
  run: |
    cd python/aibrix
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    pip install -U pip poetry
    poetry config virtualenvs.create false
    poetry install --no-root --with dev
```

That is the same window the image build hit in #2801. Poetry keeps only `uninstall` operations out of its thread pool, an `update` operation uninstalls the installed distribution before it installs the locked one, and two concurrent uninstalls read the same `site-packages` directory, so one can meet a `.dist-info` directory the other removed in between. The race is reported upstream as `python-poetry/poetry#8159` and is still open. The workflow does not pin poetry either, so `pip install -U` takes whatever is current and the drift window is wider than in the image.

### Fix

The install is serialized the same way the image is after #2801:

```yaml
poetry config virtualenvs.create false
poetry config installer.parallel false
```

The resolved package set is unchanged because the same lock file drives the same operations; only the concurrency of the install and uninstall steps is. Apart from this workflow, the only other call sites of `poetry install` are local setup steps in `python/aibrix/README.md` and `python/aibrix/AGENTS.md`.

### Evidence

- The second site was flagged in review of #2801: this workflow runs the same three steps, and it did not run on #2801 because its path filter is `python/aibrix/**`.
- In poetry 1.8.3, `poetry/installation/executor.py` computes `is_parallel_unsafe` from `job_type == "uninstall"` only, so `update` operations stay in the parallel path, and the same file sets `max_workers` to 1 when `installer.parallel` is false.
- The failure signature from the image build, a `FileNotFoundError` on a `.dist-info` directory that is not part of the failing uninstall command, is recorded in #2801.

### Test Plan

- The paths filter of this workflow includes the workflow file itself, so the three Python matrix jobs run on this change.
- `actionlint` and a YAML parse pass locally on the change.

### Related Issues

Related: #2801

title: [API] Size ModelClaim fixed-topology pools by TP × PP × PCP
body:
## Pull Request Description This PR updates ModelClaim fixed-topology validation to account for vLLM prefill context parallelism (PCP). The required GPU group size is now calculated consistently by both the ModelClaim controller and the runtime sidecar as: ```text tensor-parallel-size × pipeline-parallel-size × prefill-context-parallel-size This prevents a ModelClaim using PCP from being scheduled onto a warm Pod with fewer GPUs than the engine topology requires. The runtime repeats the same validation before activation so that direct or stale controller requests cannot bypass the topology check. The change also: - treats omitted TP, PP, PCP, and DCP values as 1; - rejects non-positive or malformed context-parallel values; - keeps data parallelism unsupported for fixed-topology pools; - adds overflow checks for the TP × PP × PCP calculation; - extends controller and runtime tests for PCP placement; - updates the ModelClaim documentation and sample topology contract. ### Why DCP is not included in the GPU topology constraint Decode context parallelism (DCP) is intentionally validated as a positive integer but is not multiplied into the required GPU count. Unlike PCP, DCP does not create an additional set of ranks. It reuses ranks from the existing TP/PCP topology during decode. Including DCP in the topology formula would therefore overestimate the number of GPUs required and reject otherwise valid warm Pods. For example, a TP=4, DCP=2 configuration still requires four GPUs, not eight. This layer is responsible for verifying the physical resource contract between a ModelClaim and a warm Pod. More specific semantic constraints between DCP and the engine topology, such as supported divisibility or grouping rules, should remain with vLLM. Those rules are engine- and version-dependent, and duplicating them in both the controller and runtime sidecar could drift from the validation performed by the engine itself. Accordingly, AIBrix only verifies that the supplied DCP value is syntactically valid and positive. It does not use DCP to calculate or further restrict the Pod GPU count. ## Related Issues Resolves: #[Insert issue number(s)] **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [Bug] Scope StormService RoleSet lookups to the owning StormService
body:
**Title:** [Bug] Scope StormService RoleSet lookups to the owning StormService

## Pull Request Description

Fixes #2779.

`getRoleSetList` listed RoleSets using only the user-supplied selector — no namespace restriction and no ownership check. `sync` (deciding how many to create), `rollout`, `finalize` (cleanup on delete) and `revision` all call it, so a StormService treated every RoleSet in the cluster whose labels happened to match as its own.

Two namespaces sharing a selector label doesn't take a misconfiguration: `samples/quickstart/pd-model.yaml` and `samples/disaggregation/vllm/1p1d.yaml` both use `app: vllm-1p1d`, both use the same object name, and neither pins a namespace, so two people each running the quickstart in their own namespace collide. What I saw on kind: the one created second brought up no RoleSets at all (the lookup already returned two), yet reported `replicas=2 ready=2`; deleting it made its finalize delete the other namespace's RoleSets, which that controller then recreated — 16 deletions and 25 Pod kills over two minutes — while its own deletion never completed.

The fix passes the StormService in, restricts the list to its namespace, and then keeps only the RoleSets it controls. Namespace scoping closes the cross-namespace case; the owner check handles overlapping selectors inside one namespace, which still reproduces once the namespace restriction is in place — I tried it, and the StormService created second owned zero RoleSets with 8 rebuilds in 60 seconds.

The reasoning: RoleSets are namespaced, their ownerReferences have pointed at the StormService in the same namespace since the controller was introduced (`e3bb459a`), the ControllerRevision and RayClusterFleet lookups already scope by namespace, and `IsControlledBy` is already used in `rayclusterfleet`.

## One thing I'd like you to decide

A RoleSet without a controller reference is now skipped and logged at V(4) rather than adopted.

The cost is that if a RoleSet ever loses its ownerReference, the controller won't take it back — it creates a new one and the old object stays around forever. Before this change, label matching picked such an object up implicitly.

I lean towards skipping, since `renderRoleSet` has always set the reference and an orphan can only come from a hand-made object or one that had its reference stripped. Doing proper adoption the way the ReplicaSet controller does is also an option, it's just a larger change. Your call.

Related to that: the existing `TestScalingPooledModeNeverCreatesSecondRoleSet` broke with this change, because its fixture builds RoleSets without an ownerReference, so the new logic filtered them out and the controller created another one. I gave the fixture an ownerReference to match what `renderRoleSet` actually does. It's a concrete example of the trade-off above.

`TestGetRoleSetList` is rewritten with seven cases: nil and invalid selector, an owned RoleSet is returned, matching labels in another namespace are excluded, matching labels owned by another StormService in the same namespace are excluded, an orphan is excluded, and a mix returns only the owned ones.

Two more:

- `TestGetRoleSetListRestrictsTheListToTheNamespace` uses an interceptor to assert the List call carries the right namespace. I added it because the cases above don't actually pin the namespace restriction — drop `InNamespace` and they still pass, since the owner filter happens to hide the cross-namespace object too.
- `TestFinalizeOnlyDeletesOwnedRoleSets` (in `sync_test.go`) runs finalize twice: the first pass deletes its own RoleSet and reports it isn't done, the second removes the finalizer, and the other namespace's RoleSet is untouched throughout.

What I ran:

```
go test ./pkg/controller/stormservice/ -skip TestControllers    all pass
golangci-lint v2.13.1                                           0 issues
```

`TestControllers` doesn't run on my machine — the envtest etcd binary is missing — and it fails the same way on unmodified code.

I mutated the fix twice to check the tests hold: dropping `InNamespace` fails the interceptor test, and dropping the owner filter fails three cases in `TestGetRoleSetList`.

Also verified end to end on a cluster, with a controller built from this branch, across three scenarios:

Two StormServices with the same selector in one namespace each own 2 RoleSets, with zero rebuilds over 60 seconds (before the change the second one owned zero and there were 8 rebuilds in 60 seconds). Deleting one leaves the other's RoleSet UIDs unchanged with zero Pods killed, and the deleted one completes immediately.

Cross-namespace, following the reproduction steps from the issue: team-a and team-b each create 2 RoleSets, and after deleting svc-b the UID hash on team-a's RoleSets doesn't change for 40 seconds, with 0 deletions and 0 Pods killed.

title: [Bug] Enforce tokenizer pool capacity during concurrent creation
body:
## Pull Request Description

Two concurrent requests for different models can both pass `TokenizerPool`'s capacity check, perform their health checks outside the lock, and then insert into the last available slot. A pool configured for one tokenizer can therefore retain two. The initial capacity check also prevents replacing an unhealthy tokenizer when the pool is full, even though replacing that model needs no additional slot.

Recheck capacity while holding the insertion lock and allow same-model replacements. Close clients discarded after a failed health check or a lost capacity race, and close the unhealthy client when replacing it.

The regression tests use a local HTTP server and a channel barrier to force both creations past their initial checks before allowing either to finish. They cover different-model capacity contention, same-model deduplication, recovery at capacity, and idle-connection cleanup.

title: [CI] Serialize the poetry install in the python image
body:
### Pull Request Description

The smoke build of the `metadata-service` image (`runtime` builds from the same Dockerfile) fails on `poetry install` with a signature that points at two different packages, one of which is not part of the command that failed:

```text
Package operations: 103 installs, 12 updates, 0 removals
  - Downgrading urllib3 (2.8.0 -> 2.6.3)
  Command '['/usr/local/bin/python3.11', '-m', 'pip', 'uninstall', 'urllib3', '-y']' returned non-zero exit status 2.
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/charset_normalizer-3.5.1.dist-info'
Cannot install urllib3.
```

Two things combine here.

The builder stage installs poetry with pip right before it runs `poetry install`, so poetry's own transitive dependencies are resolved to their latest releases (`urllib3 2.8.0`, `charset-normalizer 3.5.1`). Those are newer than the pins in `poetry.lock`, so the locked versions arrive as twelve `update` operations rather than as installs.

Poetry then runs the operations in a thread pool by default, and it keeps only `uninstall` operations out of that pool. An `update` operation uninstalls the installed distribution before it installs the locked one, so the twelve updates run `pip uninstall` against the same `site-packages` directory at the same time. A `pip uninstall` of one package reads the installed distributions it finds, so it can meet a `.dist-info` directory that another update removed in between, which is the `FileNotFoundError` above.

### Fix

The install now runs with `installer.parallel` disabled, which makes poetry execute the operations one at a time and removes the concurrency the failure needs:

```dockerfile
RUN poetry config virtualenvs.create false \
    && poetry config installer.parallel false \
    && poetry install --no-interaction --without profiling --without dev \
    && poetry build -f wheel
```

The set of packages and versions that ends up in the image is unchanged, because the same lock file drives the same operations; only the concurrency of the install and uninstall steps is. Upgrading poetry is not an option: the race is reported upstream as `python-poetry/poetry#8159`, it is still open, and the current poetry main branch does not fix it.

### Evidence

- The failing job is `Build smoke image (metadata-service)` of run `35953390757` (Installation Smoke, commit `2af26eb3`). The other jobs of that run, and the same build of the `runtime` image, passed, which fits a race rather than a broken lock file.
- In poetry 1.8.3, `poetry/installation/executor.py` computes `is_parallel_unsafe` from `operation.job_type == "uninstall"` plus a source-type check, so `update` operations stay in the parallel path, and the constructor of the executor in the same file sets `max_workers` to 1 when `installer.parallel` is false.
- `builder` stages of this Dockerfile are the only place in the repository that runs `poetry install` inside an image build (the other call sites are local setup steps in `python/aibrix/README.md`, `python/aibrix/AGENTS.md` and `python-aibrix-tests.yml`).

### Test Plan

- This pull request runs the Installation Smoke workflow, which builds both images that use this Dockerfile, so the changed line is covered by its own checks.
- The builder stage of this Dockerfile was built locally with the change: `poetry install` completed and `poetry build -f wheel` produced the wheel, after the same twelve `update` operations were printed.
- The failure is timing dependent, so a green run alone does not prove that it is gone. The evidence is that the twelve concurrent updates are now serial, and the race needs that concurrency: with `installer.parallel` disabled, poetry executes one operation at a time and no two `pip` processes touch `site-packages` at once.

### Related Issues

No tracking issue in this repository. The race is reported upstream as python-poetry/poetry#8159 and is still open there.

## Pull Request Description vLLM serves pooling models (embed/classify/score tasks) at a native /pooling endpoint, but the gateway's hardcoded path switch in validateRequestBody had no case for it, so pooling requests were rejected with 404 "not found" before ever reaching an engine. title: [Feat] Answer 503 with Retry-After for a model whose ModelClaim is not placed yet
body:
## Pull Request Description

The gateway learns about ModelClaims only from the routing annotations the controller writes on warm pods. A claim that is not placed has no pod yet. So a request for its model was answered with 400, "model ... does not exist". That is the answer for a model that nobody serves (#526). Once the claim is placed, the same request gets 503 with `Retry-After` while the engine starts.

This PR closes that gap:

- **The cache knows ModelClaim objects.** In the gateway, the Kubernetes discovery provider also watches ModelClaims. The cache keeps one record per claim: the name it serves, its phase, and the controller's reason. The reason comes from its `Scheduled` condition while it waits, or from its `Ready` condition once it has failed. A claim being deleted is forgotten, since its model is going away.
- **The gateway answers 503 for a claimed model with no pod.** The message reads like `model qwen is pending (NoMatchingPods); retry shortly`, with `Retry-After: 10`. A claim that waiting does not help gets no `Retry-After`. That is one that has to be changed first, such as one with `InvalidEngineConfig`, or one whose engine failed for good (`EngineFailed`). Other refusals get it, a failed activation included, since the controller tries it again. A model that no claim serves still gets 400.
- **Only the reason reaches the client.** The condition's full message names pods and card figures, which a client does not need.
- **RBAC.** The gateway's role can get, list and watch ModelClaims, in `config/rbac/gateway/role_gateway.yaml` and the Helm chart. The gateway lists claims once when it starts. On Forbidden or NotFound, it says so once in its log and does not watch them. Such a model is then answered with 400, as before. The ModelClaim informer is also left out of the startup sync.

There is no API change. The docs are in the "Sleeping request behavior" section of the ModelClaim guide.

Tests:

- Unit tests: the cache records, follows and forgets claims, with conditions as the controller writes them (`pkg/cache/modelclaim_test.go`). The gateway answers pending, failed and unknown models, and still wakes a sleeping claim it also knows as an object (`gateway_req_body_test.go`). The one-time list check skips claims on Forbidden or NotFound (`pkg/cache/discovery/kubernetes_test.go`). Each test was run failing before the change.
- `make test-integration-gateway` (36/36) and `make test-integration-controller` (90/90).
- A new e2e case, `TestModelClaimNotPlacedYetIsRetryable`. A claim that selects no pod is answered with 503 and `Retry-After: 10`, until it is deleted. Then it is answered with 400.

This PR does not depend on #2647.

title: [Bug] Repin the session-affinity Redis pin on a bypassed final target
body:
## Pull Request Description `sessionAffinityRouter.PostRouteUpdate` is called on paths that bypass `Route`/`resolveSessionPod`: the multi-strategy router's single-remaining-candidate fast path, and blended commits. Before this change it always persisted the final target pod with the claim write (Redis `SET NX`). If Redis already held a *different* address for that session key (for example, a load-imbalance gate had excluded the previously pinned pod, so routing moved elsewhere), the `SET NX` was silently rejected. Redis then kept the stale address even though the response's `x-session-id` header and the proxied request already pointed at the new pod. This routes `writeRepin` through a compare-and-swap and uses it from both repin call sites: - The gated refresh script from #2768 (`sessionKeyRefreshScript`) takes an optional old address (`ARGV[3]`). If Redis still holds that old address, the script replaces it with the new one and a fresh TTL (new outcome `{3}`). The existing cases are unchanged: a missing key is re-attached, a matching value has its TTL extended, and any other value is left alone and returned so the caller converges on it. A refresh is just the case where old == new; an empty `ARGV[3]` keeps the refresh behavior exactly as before. - `persistSessionKeyToRedis` takes the old address and sends both `writeRefresh` and `writeRepin` through that script, so the unconditional `SET` for repins is gone. - `resolveSessionPod` now also returns the stale address it saw (from the local cache or Redis) when it falls back to a rendezvous pick. `Route` passes that through `rememberSessionKey`. A delayed repin therefore replaces the stale pod only if Redis still holds it; if another replica has since pinned a different pod, it adopts that pin instead of overwriting it. - `PostRouteUpdate` (via `commitFinalTarget`) first reads the current pin, from the local cache when that entry is confirmed and from Redis otherwise. If it finds one, it persists with `writeRepin` against that address. If it finds nothing, it uses the claim write. Known limitation: if the Redis read in `commitFinalTarget` fails, it falls back to the claim write. That write loses to an existing pin, so the pin stays where it was until a later request. That is the same as before this change, and it never overwrites a pin. ## Validation - `go build ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...` - `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/` - `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/ -count=1` passes, including: - `TestSessionAffinityPostRouteUpdateRepinsExistingPin`, the #2772 regression test; it replaces the old test that asserted "must not overwrite". - The repin outcome tests: `TestSessionAffinityRepinSwapsObservedOldAddr`, `TestSessionAffinityRepinAttachesExpiredKey` and `TestSessionAffinityRepinLeavesFresherConcurrentWinnerAlone`. - `TestSessionAffinityResolveRepinDoesNotClobberFresherClaim`, for the delayed `resolveSessionPod` repin race. - A swap case added to `TestSessionAffinityRefreshScriptReply`. - `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/ -run 'TestSessionAffinity|TestSyncSessionKey'` passes. - `golangci-lint run ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/...` reports only a gofmt finding in `pd_bucketing_test.go`. title: [Bug] Include canonicalized tools in the prefix-match text
body:
## Pull Request Description The routing message the gateway uses for prefix matching is built from `messages[].content` only. Many chat templates render the tool definitions ahead of the conversation, so two requests with the same messages but different `tools` differ in the engine prompt from the first tokens. The gateway nevertheless treats them as a 100% prefix match and pins them to the same pod. This PR gives `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` requests a separate prefix-match text: a canonical rendering of `tools`, a single space, then the messages text. - The text is stored in a new `RoutingContext.PrefixMatchText` field and read through `PrefixText()`, which falls back to `Message` when it is empty. title: [Bug] Infer StormService mode from spec.replicas when spec.mode is unset
body:
**Title:** [Bug] Infer StormService mode from spec.replicas when spec.mode is unset

## Pull Request Description

Fixes #2780.

When a PodAutoscaler scales a single role through `subTargetSelector.roleName`, it first works out which mode the target StormService is in. `stormServiceScalingMode` used to return pooled mode whenever `spec.mode` was absent and the PodAutoscaler carried no deprecated annotation. The stormservice controller does not agree: it uses `ResolvedMode()`, where `replicas > 1` means replica mode.

Once the autoscaler settles on pooled, what it reads and what it writes stop being the same quantity. It reads `status.roleStatuses[role].replicas`, which is the role summed over every RoleSet, and writes `spec.template.spec.roles[role].replicas`, which the controller copies into each RoleSet. The two differ by the number of RoleSets, so it can never converge. On kind, with `replicas: 3` and `maxReplicas: 10`, the decode role ended up at 30 Pods while the PodAutoscaler kept reporting `actualScale=30 desiredScale=10`, rewriting the template on every reconcile and rebuilding the RoleSets as it went.

The change is one line: when neither the mode nor the annotation is present, fall back to `ss.Spec.ResolvedMode()`, which is the same inference the controller applies. That is the compatibility rule #2449 recorded in its backward-compatibility section. A declared `spec.mode` and the deprecated annotation keep their precedence.

One behaviour change worth calling out: `annotation: pool` combined with `replicas > 1` now resolves to replica mode. That combination contradicts itself (`pool` is not a valid value either — the code only ever matched `replica`), and I added a case to pin the new behaviour down. Happy to keep it pooled instead if you would rather not change it.

## Tests

Six cases added to the `TestStormServiceScalingMode` table:

- no mode with `replicas` of 3, 1 and 0
- `spec.mode: Pooled` with `replicas: 3` stays pooled
- annotation `replica` with `replicas: 1` stays replica
- annotation `pool` with `replicas: 3` infers replica

The last three guard the precedence order, so the fallback is the only thing that moved. The eight existing cases are untouched.

Two more tests cover the read and write paths:

- `TestGetCurrentReplicasInferredReplicaMode` deliberately sets `spec.replicas=3` against an aggregated status of 6 and asserts the autoscaler reads 3
- `TestSetDesiredReplicasInferredReplicaMode` asserts `spec.replicas` is what changes and the role replicas in the template are left alone

What I ran:

```
go test ./pkg/controller/podautoscaler/...      all pass
golangci-lint v2.13.1                           0 issues
```

I also reverted the one line to the old behaviour to check the tests actually catch this: the four new cases fail and the eight existing ones still pass.

Verified on a cluster too. With the patched controller and the same setup, `spec.replicas` climbs from 3 to 10 and stops, the template's `decode: 2` is never touched, and the following two minutes show zero RoleSet rebuilds and zero rescale calls.

## Related Issues

Resolves: #2780

title: [Feat] Accept workers and prefill/decode worker keys in the static config
body:
### Pull Request Description

The static endpoints file is the first thing a new deployment writes, and its shape depends on where the reader comes from. The TRT-LLM recipes spell the simple backend list `workers` and the disaggregated pair `prefill_workers` and `decode_workers`, while this repository spells the same two things `endpoints` and a `rolesets` list whose entries carry a name, a prefill list and a decode list.

This is the static config piece of #2031, which the issue thread asked to handle first. The provider itself was already renamed to `StaticProvider`, so what is left on the naming side is the file format:

- `workers` is accepted as an alias of `endpoints`.
- `prefill_workers` and `decode_workers` are accepted as the shorthand for a single roleset named `default`.
- The existing `endpoints` and `rolesets` keys keep working, so no deployment has to move, and the `rolesets` form stays the way to express multiple groups or an explicit group name.

`StaticModelConfig.resolve()` turns whichever spelling the file uses into the `(endpoints, rolesets)` pair the provider already built pods from, so the cache, the pod labels and the PD router are untouched. `default` is the roleset name the shipped configs and the PD docs already used, and the role labels stay an implementation detail of the provider, as discussed in the issue.

Nothing is guessed silently: the three combinations that cannot be reconciled, `endpoints` with `workers`, `rolesets` with the shorthand, and the non-disaggregated form with the disaggregated one, fail the load with a message that names the model.

The load also got the checks the format change left open: a model with an empty name, which produced pods named `-vllm-0` with an empty `model.aibrix.ai/name` that nothing could route to, and a model with no backends at all, which loaded cleanly and contributed no pods. Both fail the load now. The shorthand must list both sides, and a named roleset must declare at least one worker, so a config that could never be routed fails at load instead of loading into a model that serves nothing.

### Review guide

Two files carry the code change, the rest are the examples and docs a user copies from:

1. `pkg/cache/discovery/static.go` (+88/-10) - the three new fields, `resolve()` and `load()` switching to it. `defaultRoleSetName` sits with the provider constants because the roleset name is the pairing key the PD router groups pods by.
2. `pkg/cache/discovery/static_test.go` (+239) - the two aliases, the shorthand and its both-sides rule, the conflict cases, and the required-field cases.
3. `deployment/local/configs/endpoints.yaml`, `deployment/standalone/configs/endpoints.yaml`, `deployment/standalone/configs/endpoints-pd.yaml`, `deployment/local/README.md`, `deployment/standalone/README.md`, `docs/source/getting_started/installation/local-mode.rst`, `pkg/cache/discovery/README.md` - rewritten to the new spelling, with the `rolesets` form kept documented.

### Test Plan

- `go test ./pkg/cache/discovery/... -count=1` passes: 16 tests, six of them new.
- `gofmt -l` empty, `go vet ./pkg/cache/discovery/...` passes, `golangci-lint` v2.13.1 reports 0 issues on the package.
- The three shipped example configs are parsed through the provider and yield 1, 1 and 2 pods (1 prefill, 1 decode).
- `sphinx-build -b html -W --keep-going docs/source docs/_build/html` passes with no warnings.

### Related Issues

Addresses the static config part of #2031.

title: [API][Docs] Place a ModelClaim only where its card has room, and hold each engine to its share
body:
## Pull Request Description The controller picks a warm pod and starts the engine, and only finds out that the model does not fit when the engine runs out of memory. By then, the claim has spent its restart budget on that one pod, and placement does not try another. When several models share a card, nothing divides it between them either. Each engine starts under whatever limit its own KV allocator chose, which is most of the card. This PR makes placement answer "does it fit" before `Activate`, and makes the answer hold afterwards. A claim declares what one instance costs on a GPU. The controller keeps an account per card, and admits a model only where the account shows room. When the model lands, the card is divided between the engines on it, and each engine stays routable only while it is held to its share. ### What a claim declares ```yaml spec: perGPU: maximumFootprint: 30Gi # non-KV memory one instance holds on a device kvFloor: 10Gi # the KV one instance needs to serve at all ``` Neither figure can be derived from the artifact. Most of the gap between an artifact and what an engine holds is allocator retention, which does not scale with the weights. Declaring more than an instance needs wastes room and is safe. Declaring less is not. `perGPU` is optional in the schema. A claim without it, or with a figure that is not positive, is accepted and not placed. Its `Scheduled` condition reads `InvalidPerGPU` and names the figure. When `perGPU` is given, both figures are required. The field is optional so that a claim stored before it existed stays valid. A required field would make the API server refuse every update to such a claim except to its status. Without CRD validation ratcheting, which is on by default only from Kubernetes 1.30, that includes removing the controller's finalizer, so the claim could not be deleted. An engine that such a claim already runs keeps its route, and its card is left unaccountable until the claim declares its cost. ### What the control plane works out | Name | Source | What it is | |---|---|---| | `hbmUsableBytes` | runtime | NVML v2 total, less what the driver reserves. A multi-GPU pod is sized by its smallest card. | | `kvUsedBytes` | runtime | The KV an engine has mapped in kvcached, pages in use and in reserve. | | `minimumReserveBytes` | derived | `maximumFootprint + kvFloor`. What one instance takes and does not give back while it is awake. | | `kvHeldBytes` | derived, per engine | `max(kvFloor, kvUsedBytes)`. Lowering a KV limit evicts nothing, so an engine keeps at least this. | | `maximumRoomBytes` | derived | `hbmUsableBytes` less every recorded instance's `maximumFootprint + kvFloor`. The most the card could ever offer. | | `heldRoomBytes` | derived | `hbmUsableBytes` less every recorded instance's `maximumFootprint + kvHeldBytes`. What the card can offer now. | | `kvLimitBytes` | derived, per engine | `kvHeldBytes` plus its part of what is left over. Recorded in `status.instances[].kvLimitBytes`. | Nothing here reads free HBM. An instance is charged from the moment it is recorded in `status`, so an engine that is still loading is never invisible to the next admission. The snapshot covers the other direction: a live engine that no recorded instance answers for makes its card unaccountable. A pod is accounted for if it requests `nvidia.com/gpu` or its runtime reports GPUs. The second covers GPUs from a dynamic resource claim. ### How a model is placed ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Claim to place:
minimumReserveBytes"] --> B{"Can the card
be accounted for?"} B -- "no: runtime silent, card unmeasured,
a claim there declares nothing usable,
or an engine answers to no claim" --> N["Try the next pod"] B -- yes --> C{"maximumRoomBytes at least
minimumReserveBytes?"} C -- no --> N C -- yes --> D{"heldRoomBytes at least
minimumReserveBytes?"} D -- no --> N D -- yes --> E["Rank the admitted pods"] E --> F["Divide the card: write the limits
(shrinks first), read them back,
then record them"] F -- "a write or the read-back failed" --> N F -- confirmed --> G["Record the new instance with
its limit, then Activate"] G --> H["Routable only once its
own limit is in force"] N -- "no pod left" --> P["Stay Pending with the reason,
and try again on the next pass"] ``` The first gate asks whether the card could ever hold the model, with every engine squeezed to its floor. A card that fails it will not take the model, however long the claim waits. The second gate asks whether the card can hold the model now. Lowering a limit does not evict a mapped page, so a card whose room is held by the engines on it fails the second gate and not the first. The division keeps each engine's `kvHeldBytes`, and shares out the rest by demand. An engine's weight is one plus its running and waiting requests, with the requests capped at four, as the pool policy caps them. The limits spend the card exactly, so an engine that grows into its new limit cannot grow into a neighbour's memory. Shrinks are written before grows. A write alone proves nothing: kvcached's CLI exits 0 even when the segment does not exist. So the limits are read back from a fresh snapshot. Only then are they recorded on the claims, with the new instance last. A division that fails part way changes no record. Ranking uses the same account. A pod that already has the artifact ranks first. Every ranked pod has passed both gates, so the choice is between cards that all fit, and a cached artifact saves the download. Next comes the roomiest card by `maximumRoomBytes`, which does not move with traffic. On the roomiest card, the neighbours give up the least when it is divided. Free HBM and the older tie-breakers only break ties. ### Holding each engine to its limit An engine becomes routable only when the limit in its segment is the one its instance records. It stays routable only while that limit is no larger than the record. An engine held to more, as when a restart puts its allocator's default back, is taken off the route with a `KVLimitNotHeld` Event. It is pulled back to its record, and then routed again. An instance is recorded before its engine starts, so the account charges it at once. Sometimes the runtime then has no engine for it, for example if the controller stopped between the two steps. The controller then starts the engine again. This is safe, because the runtime starts a model only once. If the start fails, the instance is dropped and the card is freed. The health loop always shrinks an engine to its record. It grows an engine only while the engine is off the route. A larger record for a serving engine comes from a division whose writes have not all landed, and growing it outside that order could hand it memory that a neighbour has not given back. The `reclaim` policy of the pool annotation stands down on any pod where a claim records a limit, since two writers on one allocator would only overwrite each other. The feature page marks `reclaim` as superseded. ### What an operator sees A refusal names the roomiest pod that still could not hold the model, the gate it failed, and that card's account: ``` no warm pod can hold this model, which needs 40.0 GiB on a card: warm-runtime-pool-zeyu-69846d7fdf-nxk2t can offer at most 15.3 GiB, even with every engine on it at its floor (the card holds 95.3 GiB, and 80.0 GiB of it is promised to 2 instance(s)) ``` The cards are blamed only when they are the reason. With no candidate at all, or with the model already on every candidate, the message stays the generic one, so an operator is not sent to look at GPU memory. `Scheduled` is set to `True` with reason `Placed` once an instance is recorded. The Events are `InvalidPerGPU`, `NoMatchingPods`, `KVLimitSet` (on the claim of each engine a division moved), `KVLimitFailed` and `KVLimitNotHeld`. A refusal Event is raised only when the refusal changes. ### Checked on hardware This branch as it stands ran on one H20, which the runtime measures at 95.33 GiB usable. Two 1.5B models each declared `maximumFootprint: 30Gi` and `kvFloor: 10Gi`. - kvcached started the first engine at 80.0 GiB. It was held to 65.3 GiB, the card less its footprint, before it was routable. - When the second model arrived, the first engine was held to 17.7 GiB and read back before the second was recorded. It kept its route throughout. The second engine was pulled from 80.0 GiB to 17.7 GiB before it was routable. The footprints and the limits came to 95.33 GiB exactly. - A third claim of the same size was refused with the message above. It was tried again every 10 seconds, and no engine was started for it. After the first claim was deleted, the third was placed within a few seconds of the first engine exiting. - A 21.7 GiB limit was written into a serving engine behind the controller's back. The engine was taken off the route, pulled back to 17.7 GiB, and routed again within about 2 seconds. Its neighbour was untouched. - A claim with no `perGPU`, and one with `kvFloor: "0"`, were both accepted and never placed, with one `InvalidPerGPU` Event each. A `perGPU` without its `kvFloor` was refused by the API server. - An engine was stopped through the runtime, without the controller. The controller started it again 4 seconds later. The new engine came up at 80.0 GiB and was pulled down to its record of 17.7 GiB. Only then was it routed, 48 seconds after the stop. Its neighbour kept its route. The integration suite runs the real controller against a real API server. Its ten ModelClaim specs include a claim with no `perGPU`. ### What this PR does not do The first two are the next PRs under #2290, each with its own issue. - The card is divided only when a model is placed on it. When a model leaves, its room waits for the next model placed on that card. Dividing a card again on a timer, and whenever the engines on it change, is online KV budgeting. - A claim that cannot be placed is tried again every 10 seconds, whatever the reason. Backing off, and saying when no card could ever hold the model, is the PR after that. - An engine starts under its allocator's own default, and it is pulled down once it is ready (#2770). It is not routable before then, so it takes no traffic, but nothing stops it from mapping more while it loads. - Sleeping does not free a seat. An instance that is asleep keeps its place in the account at its full declared cost, because the assignment has to survive the sleep for a wake to find its engine again. - The declaration is trusted. Checking it against what an engine actually uses needs `hbm_peak_bytes`, which reads 0 today. NVML reports host PIDs, and the runtime walks the container's process tree. ## Related Issues Resolves: #2744 Part of #2290 Related: #2770 Supersedes #2745, as agreed with @jiangxiaobin96, who co-authored the commits that declare the per-GPU cost and admit against it.

title: [Bug] Key gateway rate history by namespace/name
body:
## Pull Request Description The gateway keeps a process-wide rate history (`rateCalculator` in `pkg/cache`) for rates it derives from counters. Its keys used the bare pod name: - `calculateRate1m`: `podName//metric`, with no namespace and no model. It feeds `RealtimeRunningRequestsDrainRate1m` (PD decode drain-rate scoring) and `RealtimeOutputTokenRateEWMA` (the load-balance router's capacity estimate). - `calculatePerSecondRate`: `podName/model/metric`. It feeds `AvgPromptThroughputToksPerS` / `AvgGenerationThroughputToksPerS` (PD decode throughput scoring). Same-named pods in different namespaces are common when a controller names pods by index, such as StatefulSet or LeaderWorkerSet. Those pods shared one series: - A pod's rate could be computed against a snapshot of the other pod's counter. - A smaller counter from the other pod was read as a counter reset, so the pod's whole counter value was used as the delta. For `calculateRate1m` this happened even across models. In a local test with interleaved updates, `calculatePerSecondRate` reported about 994,000/s for a pod whose true rate was about 500/s. Deleting a pod also purged the history of its same-named twin, because `PurgeEntriesForPod` matched on the name only. The history is in-memory only, so the new key format needs no migration. **Tests:** - the per-second rate and the 1-minute rate stay separate for same-named pods in two namespaces - purging one pod leaves its same-named twin and a pod whose name shares a prefix (`decode-0` vs `decode-00`) untouched - all three tests fail when the namespace is dropped from the key Verification: - `go test -race ./pkg/cache/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...` passes - golangci-lint reports no issues ## Related Issues Part of #2800 (the High item). title: [Misc] Pin the SLOQueue ordering contract and cover the policy switch matrix
body:
### Pull Request Description

`Peek` picked the next request to serve with a comparator that had no tie-break, and sorted each candidate's profile list with an unstable comparison, so equal ranks left the pick to the `sync.Map` iteration order that collects the subqueue candidates. The same queued set could therefore be served in a different order from one gateway process to the next. This change pins the order `Peek` uses and covers it with tests.

- Candidates are ordered by the rank of the candidate's most relaxing profile, descending: the request closest to a violation is served first. Equal finite ranks break on arrival time (FIFO) and then on the subqueue key, which is unique within one `Peek`, so the order is total. A NaN rank cannot be compared, so it sorts after every comparable rank and such a candidate is served last; two NaN ranks fall back to arrival time and then to the subqueue key.
- A candidate's profiles are ordered by rank ascending with the profile key as tie-break. That is the order the relaxer walks when it stops before the first profile whose rank is above zero, so the walk no longer depends on how pod indexes are enumerated.
- The queue service time in the queue-wide rank keeps its `(Len()-1)/throughput` meaning and now says so in the comment: `Len()` counts the head, whose own serving time is accounted separately.

### Switch matrix

The four policy switches live on a `queueOptions` struct on `SLOQueue`, so every branch is reachable from tests. Production runs the shipped values, which `NewSLOQueue` writes down once:

| Switch | Default | `true` | `false` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fifoOnNonSLOViolation` | `false` | candidates that both rank below zero are served in arrival order | candidates are always compared by rank |
| `queueOverallSLO` | `false` | rank accounts for the requests queued behind the head (`queueRank`) | rank is computed per request (`rank`) |
| `monogenousGPURouting` | `true` | a candidate is routed per deployment profile, most relaxing first | a candidate is routed against the whole pod set in one call |
| `monogenousGPURoutingOnly` | `false` | only the most relaxing profile is tried | profiles are tried until one succeeds or the first violating one is reached |

`monogenousGPURoutingOnly` is read only inside the `monogenousGPURouting` branch, so it has no effect unless profile routing is on.

### Behavior change

Two observable changes. Equal finite ranks previously followed the candidate collection order, which is the `sync.Map` iteration order and changes between processes, and now follow arrival time and then the subqueue key. A NaN rank previously left the order undefined and now sorts after every comparable rank. NaN last is a policy choice: `LatencySeconds` returns a NaN cell with a nil error for an unmeasured bucket, so the request stays in the ranked set, an unknown rank is the least urgent rather than the most urgent, and a candidate whose every profile is NaN is served in the same last place. The tie-break reads the request's `RequestTime`, the same field the FIFO branch used, which is stable for the duration of a `Peek`. Rank differences between comparable ranks are unaffected, so no request that ranked higher before is served later now.

### Review guide

The change is 634 lines across three files, and the new spec file is most of it. Reading order:

1. `pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/slo_queue.go` (+105/-23) - the whole change lives here: `profileLess` and `candidateLess` (the two comparators that replace `higherRank`), the NaN-first decisions inside them, and how `Peek` uses them.
2. `pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/slo_queue_ordering_test.go` (new, 482, Ginkgo) - 15 specs in two groups: the `SLOQueue ordering contract` group covers the end-to-end tie, the comparator-level tie-breaks under an adversarial input order, and the NaN cases (a NaN rank, two NaN ranks, a NaN profile the relaxer walks into); the `SLOQueue policy switches` group covers the switch matrix above. The file also owns the shared fixtures (`rankedRequestAt`, `installProfiles`, `newTestSLOQueueWithProvider`, `recordingPodList`).
3. `pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/slo_queue_test.go` (+47/-34) - one spec is rewritten at the comparator level (the old `higherRank` difference spec becomes the rank, arrival time, subqueue key spec) and the helpers now delegate to the new file; no other expectation changes.

What is worth checking closely: (a) both comparators are a strict weak ordering for every pair of ranks, including two NaNs; (b) the tie-break reads only `RequestTime` and the subqueue key, so one `Peek` sees one order; (c) no request that ranked higher before is served later now.

### Test Plan

- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/... -race -count=1` passes.
- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... -count=1` passes.
- `golangci-lint` v2.13.1 on the package reports 0 issues.
- `slo_queue_ordering_test.go` covers the tie contract end to end (`serves the older candidate when all candidates rank the same`, with the ranks asserted to be equal so the fixture cannot silently stop being a tie) and at the comparator level with an adversarial input order for both the arrival-time and subqueue-key fallbacks, plus the NaN gaps: equal finite profile ranks break on the profile key, two all-NaN candidates break on arrival time, and the relaxer walks into a NaN profile once every comparable rank has passed its stop point.
- The remaining specs cover the relaxer attempt order and its stop before the violating profile, the whole-pod-set branch, the FIFO branch with two negative ranks, the queue-wide rank branch that flips the pick against the per-request rank, and the cross-profile pick whose winning candidate starts at its most relaxing profile.
- The tie specs need one `Peek` over an adversarial sort order each, with no repeated loop.
- Mutation checks on the change: removing the tie-break turns four ordering specs red, and dropping the NaN branch from either comparator turns the matching NaN ordering spec red.

### Related Issues

None. The gap was found while reading the SLO queue, and there is no tracking issue for it.

title: [Feat] Support TensorRT-LLM generation-first (parallel) P/D routing
body:
## Pull Request Description

Adds opt-in **generation-first (parallel) P/D scheduling for TensorRT-LLM**, closing the gap described in #2018. The PD router previously only supported context-first scheduling (prefill → wait for response → decode).

## Related Issues

Resolves: #2018

With `AIBRIX_TRT_SCHEDULE_STYLE=generation_first`, the gateway:

1. resolves the selected CTX worker's `/server_info` (`ctx_info_endpoint`, `ctx_dp_rank`, optional `encoded_opaque_state`) through a lazily populated cache (single-flighted per worker incarnation, 1-minute TTL, 1024-entry bound, 3-second lookup timeout, redirects rejected, 1 MiB response cap);
2. builds **both** request bodies up front from one shared integer `disagg_request_id`, with `schedule_style: 1` (TRT-LLM `GENERATION_FIRST`) inside `disaggregated_params`;
3. starts the `context_only` request in a goroutine and returns the decode target plus the already-mutated `generation_only` body to Envoy, so both legs overlap.

The default is unchanged: `context_first` stays the default, the mode is an immutable router-local handler (the shared engine registry is never mutated, so no other router or request is affected), and vLLM, SGLang and combined-pod routing take the same paths as before.

### Files

| Area | Files |
|------|-------|
| Mode selection / request building | `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/engine/trtllm.go`, `pd_disaggregation.go` |
| CTX metadata cache | `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/engine/trtllm_server_info.go` |
| Async dispatch + failure handling | `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/prefill/default.go`, `pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway_pd_fail_fast.go` |
| Tests | `pd/engine/trtllm_generation_first_test.go`, `pd/engine/trtllm_server_info_test.go`, `pd/prefill/trtllm_test.go`, `pd_trt_generation_first_test.go`, `gateway_pd_fail_fast_test.go` |
| Docs / sample | `pd_readme.md`, `docs/source/features/pd-disaggregation.rst`, `samples/quickstart/tensorrt/README.md`, `samples/quickstart/tensorrt/tensor-rt-pd.yaml` |

### Deliberate differences from the issue text

The issue describes a proxy that issues both requests itself. Three implementation choices differ, all because of how AIBrix dispatches PD today:

1. **Lazy per-worker `/server_info` load, not an init-time crawl.** The gateway's pod cache does not contain future/autoscaled CTX pods at router construction. The cache is created at init and filled for the selected worker before either leg is dispatched.
2. **The router never POSTs the decode leg.** In AIBrix the decode request is forwarded by Envoy; the router returns the decode address and the mutated body (`gateway_req_body.go`). This is the same mechanism context-first, vLLM and SGLang use, and it is what makes the two legs overlap. There is consequently no gateway-side ordering guarantee between the CTX POST and Envoy's GEN forward.
3. **`ctx_dp_rank` is taken from the selected worker's own `/server_info`** instead of a router-maintained rank table, so a rank can never be applied to a different worker. Rank `0` is never substituted for missing data: a missing/`null` rank is an error and routing fails before dispatch.

### Configuration

```yaml
# gateway plugin only, not the model containers
- name: AIBRIX_TRT_SCHEDULE_STYLE
  value: "generation_first"   # or context_first (default)
```

An unrecognized value is logged and leaves the router on `context_first`, matching the other env-driven knobs in this package. `AIBRIX_TRT_MACHINE_ID` should differ per gateway process sharing TRT workers, as with context-first.

**Worker prerequisite:** both roles must run TRT-LLM's **Python** KV-cache transceiver (`cache_transceiver_config: {backend: DEFAULT|NIXL, transceiver_runtime: PYTHON}`). Only that transceiver implements the generation-first metadata — `BindKvCacheTransceiver.get_disaggregated_params()` returns `{}` in v1.3.0rc8 — so a worker on the default C++ transceiver answers `/server_info` with an empty `disaggregated_params` and cannot be used for this mode. The sample now sets this, and the router's error message names the cause when it sees an empty `disaggregated_params`.

### Failure handling

The CTX request keeps the client's cancellation and the existing prefill timeout, and reports failures through the per-incarnation PD leg state (never through the pooled `RoutingContext`). TRT-LLM has no SGLang `rid`/`/abort_request` contract, so no abort POST is made: the gateway instead fails/resets the Envoy stream and relies on TRT-LLM cancelling the promise on HTTP disconnect. Because TRT can send SSE headers before KV is available, a terminal CTX failure after headers resets the stream rather than being treated as "decode is healthy" — this can truncate an already-streaming response, but it cannot leave a generation leg waiting indefinitely for KV.

### Tests run

```

title: [Feat] Scope the VTC token tracker per profile
body:
### Pull Request Description

#2786 gave a model config profile a `routingConfig` whose knobs override the gateway's environment defaults for that profile's requests. The knobs that configure state shared by every model of a gateway process were left out of it, and for a good reason: a value read per request cannot be applied to an already built tracker, cache or timer. This change scopes the group whose state can be built per configuration, the VTC token tracker:

| Profile field | What it now bounds for this profile's requests |
| --- | --- |
| `vtc.inputTokenWeight`, `vtc.outputTokenWeight` | the weights of the VTC token tracker they use |
| `vtc.tokenTrackerWindowSize`, `vtc.tokenTrackerTimeUnit`, `vtc.tokenTrackerMinTokens`, `vtc.tokenTrackerMaxTokens` | the sliding window, its bucket size, and the token floors reported while the window holds little activity |

The remaining state-sharing knobs of #1961 stay environment-only and no longer appear in the profile config. A value that acts as a ceiling on state every profile shares, the session-affinity pin cache, the routing-string caches or the token-load session table, cannot be honored per request, because the count it would be compared against is the process-wide one. The preble histogram window and its eviction loop need per-profile histograms and eviction schedules, which is a design of its own. `pkg/types/routing_knobs.go` carries the rule the fields follow: a state-sharing knob keeps a profile field only where the read site can give the profile its own instance of that state, keyed by the resolved values.

### Semantics

- **Scoping, not retuning.** A profile that sets one of these knobs does not touch the shared instance: the gateway builds a tracker keyed by the resolved values, so profiles that agree share one and a profile that sets none reads the shared tracker exactly as before. The number of instances is tied to the distinct configurations rather than to the number of profiles.
- **Bounded.** VTC trackers are capped at 16 per process. Past the cap a request keeps the shared tracker, and it is both scored and priced with that tracker's own floors and weights rather than the profile's, which is the behaviour it had before this change. A request never fails because too many profiles asked for their own tracker, and the cap is logged once.
- **No cost until asked.** A request whose profile sets none of the six knobs reads the same tracker object as before, and the default path only compares the resolved values.
- **Weights belong to their scope.** The two token weights are baked into a tracker, so a profile that changes one gets a tracker of its own instead of mixing its counts with the shared tracker's; they are not multipliers that could be applied at read time.
- **`WithWindowSize` stops leaking.** The option used to overwrite the process-wide default, so one tracker built with a 100 ms window silently retuned every tracker built afterwards. It now configures the tracker it is applied to and leaves the default alone.

### Implementation

- `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/vtc/tracker_scope.go` adds the scope key (window, unit, floors and the two weights) and the bounded registry that builds one tracker per scope outside the lock and keeps the winner of a race.
- `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/vtc/vtc_basic.go` resolves the request to its tracker once per routing pass (`trackerFor`), which returns the tracker together with the knobs it was built from, and both the route and the scoring path size the bucket from those knobs. `ScoreAll` still never updates the tracker it scores with, so scoring a candidate cannot commit a request the blend may route elsewhere.
- `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/vtc/token_tracker.go` takes the window, floors and unit from the knobs it is constructed with (`NewScopedInMemorySlidingWindowTokenTracker`), and the process-wide constructor now goes through the same path with the environment knobs.
- `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/profile_knobs.go` resolves and validates the six fields, dropping a value the matching environment variable would reject.
- `pkg/plugins/gateway/ENV_VARS.md` and `docs/source/features/gateway-plugins.rst` move the six knobs into the profile tables and keep the other state-sharing knobs in the environment-only lists.

### Test Plan

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/types/...`, `gofmt -l`, `make licensecheck` and `make lint` (golangci-lint v2.13.1, 0 issues) are clean.
- `go test ./pkg/types/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...` passes, plus a focused `-race` run over the new scope tests.
- `vtc/vtc_scope_test.go` covers the default path sharing one tracker object, two profiles with the same knobs sharing one tracker while a different weight resolves a different one, the trackers' state (counts, floors, weights) staying isolated, the 16-scope bound falling back to the shared tracker with the request still routable and scored with that tracker's floors, 16 concurrent requests of one profile ending on the same tracker, and `WithWindowSize` no longer retuning the process default.
- `routing_profile_knobs_test.go` covers the six fields end to end through `ResolveRoutingOverrides`: the accepted values, every field in the all-values-rejected case, and that `vtc.tokenTrackerTimeUnit` lands only for a name the tracker knows instead of being normalized to minutes.

### Related Issues

Refs #1961
