title: [Bug] Stop LocalStorage rewriting newlines in stored text objects
body:
## The bug

`LocalStorage._write_file` writes text objects through a text-mode handle:

```python
with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(str(reader))
```

Without `newline=""`, Python translates every `"\n"` written to `os.linesep`. On Windows that means a stored text object comes back with `\r\n`, so `put_object(x)` followed by `get_object()` does not return `x`. Nothing raises — the corruption is silent, and `LocalStorage` is the default local-development backend.

Minimal repro, independent of aibrix:

```python
fd, p = tempfile.mkstemp()
with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("a\nb")
open(p, "rb").read()      # b'a\r\nb' on Windows, b'a\nb' with newline=""
```

## Why it has gone unnoticed

`os.linesep` is `"\n"` on Linux, so the translation is a no-op there and CI stays green. It is only observable on Windows, where it already makes an existing spec fail:

```
tests/storage/test_reader.py::TestReaderIntegration::test_reader_with_different_file_types_in_storage
AssertionError: assert b'name,age\r\nAlice,30\r\nBob,25' == b'name,age\nAlice,30\nBob,25'
```

## The fix

Pass `newline=""` so the bytes are written exactly as given. That is the standard way to ask Python for no newline translation — the same thing the `csv` module's docs require when opening files.

Scope is deliberately one line. `_write_json_file` uses the same text-mode pattern but is not affected: `json.dump` emits no bare newlines and escapes `\n` inside values, so nothing reaches the translation layer. Happy to harden it defensively in a follow-up if maintainers prefer.

## Tests

Added `test_text_content_round_trips_without_newline_translation`, which stores a string containing `\n`, reads it back, and asserts the bytes are unchanged. Removing `newline=""` again turns it red on Windows with a diagnostic failure:

```
assert b'first\r\nsecond\r\nthird' == b'first\nsecond\nthird'
```

**One honest limitation:** this spec cannot fail on Linux CI, for the same reason the bug is invisible there. I could not find a way to catch it on Linux without asserting on the implementation (e.g. mocking `os.fdopen` and checking the arguments), which seemed worse than leaving it platform-gated. The structural answer is Windows coverage in CI, which is beyond this PR — flagging it rather than pretending the spec guards every platform.

With the fix, `pytest tests/storage` is 156 passed / 13 skipped on Windows; previously 154 passed / 1 failed.

title: [Misc] Harden _write_json_file against newline translation
body:
What

Follow-up to the non-blocking nit on [#2757](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/2757): _write_json_file opens its temp file in text mode without newline="", the same pattern that caused the newline rewriting fixed there.

Why it is safe today, and why it is worth hardening

json.dump is called without indent, so it emits a single compact line with no bare \n, and any newline inside a string value is escaped as \\n. Nothing reaches the text layer for Python to translate, so the current behaviour is correct on every platform.

The risk is a future edit. The moment someone adds indent= to make the metadata readable, json.dump starts emitting real newlines, and on Windows those become \r\n — the exact failure mode #2757 fixed one branch above. Passing newline="" now means that change cannot reintroduce it.

No new test, deliberately

There is no input that distinguishes the two forms today: with json.dump emitting no bare newlines, the bytes written are identical with and without the argument. A test that fails before this change and passes after it cannot be written — which is itself the evidence that this is hardening rather than a bug fix.

Evidence that behaviour is unchanged

pytest tests/storage is 156 passed, 13 skipped on Windows, identical to before the change.

title: [Misc] Cover the growing half of the RoundRobin channel-set spec
body:
## What

Follow-up to the non-blocking nit on #2752.

`test_cursor_survives_the_channel_set_growing_and_shrinking` is named for the cursor tolerating the reachable set **both** growing and shrinking, and that is what the `RoundRobin` docstring promises:

> Tolerates the set growing/shrinking between calls (the cursor is taken modulo the live length)

But the sequence only ever shrank — `3 → 2 → 1`. The growing half of the claim was never exercised, so the spec's name and comment promised more than the assertions delivered.

## The change

Grow the set to four channels before shrinking it: `3 → 4 → 2 → 1`.

| call | live length | cursor before | `cursor % len` | picked | cursor after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | 0 | 0 | first | 1 |
| 2 | **4** | 1 | 1 | second | 2 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | 0 | first | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 0 | first | 0 |

The growth step is deliberately placed where the cursor is non-zero. With a cursor of 0 the assertion would hold for any list length — `0 % anything` is `0` — so it would not actually demonstrate that the modulo tracks the live length.

The comment is updated to walk all four steps, since it described the old three-step sequence.

## Test plan

```
pytest tests/batch/client/test_policy.py -v
ruff check tests/batch/client/test_policy.py
mypy tests/batch/client/test_policy.py
```

All pass. Test-only; no production code is touched.

title: [Feat] Map the request priority tier to the vLLM request priority
body:
### Pull Request Description

Requests that share a model endpoint have different latency needs, and there is currently no way for a caller to say which one it is. An interactive turn can end up queued behind a nightly batch backfill even though the batch job would be perfectly happy to wait.

This adds the opt-in mapping proposed in #2286, with the v0 scope that was stated there. When `AIBRIX_PRIORITY_TIER_ENABLED=true`, a request carrying the `x-aibrix-priority-tier` header has the matching value written into the `priority` field of its backend request body:

| `x-aibrix-priority-tier` | `priority` | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `batch` | `100` | Below the engine default of `0`, so batch work yields to interactive requests. |
| `background` | `1000` | Yields to both interactive and `batch` work. |
| _(other or missing)_ | _(unchanged)_ | Forwarded untouched. |

vLLM serves smaller `priority` values first, so both entries sit below the engine default of `0` and the mapping can only de-prioritize. There is no path by which enabling this feature pulls a request ahead of one that did not set a tier, which is what makes it safe to switch on for a shared endpoint. The engine does the actual scheduling, so vLLM deployments need a priority-aware scheduler (`--scheduling-policy=priority`) for the field to have an effect.

### Semantics

- **Off by default.** While `AIBRIX_PRIORITY_TIER_ENABLED` is unset or `false`, the header is ignored and request bodies are forwarded byte for byte. There is no behavior change for existing deployments.
- **De-prioritize only.** The table has no value that outranks a request without a tier. A latency-sensitive tier can get an explicit head start later if that is wanted; doing it in a separate change keeps this one incapable of delaying traffic that opted out of nothing.
- **The caller wins.** A `priority` already present in the request body is never overwritten, so a client can pick a value for a tier the table maps, or use the field directly for a tier it does not.
- **Fail-open.** Only a well formed JSON object is extended. An empty body, JSON `null`, a JSON string or array, a truncated body, and the non-JSON endpoints such as the multipart audio and video paths are forwarded byte for byte, and none of that relies on `sjson` error behaviour. The tier is a hint and never fails or blocks a request.
- **No new artifact.** The tier rides on a request header rather than a new CRD or profile field, which keeps this usable from any client the gateway already serves.
- Tier names are matched case-insensitively, and the value is trimmed where the header is recorded on the routing context.

### Implementation

- `pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway_req_priority.go` holds the tier table and the rewrite. The object guard runs first, then the body is edited in place on `routingCtx.ReqBody` with `sjson`, the same helper the PD path uses, so no field other than `priority` changes.
- `gateway_req_headers.go` records the trimmed header value on the routing context.
- `gateway_req_body.go` applies the mapping before routing, and forwards the routing context body with a `content-length` computed from it. The placement matters twice over:
  - the PD router builds the prefill payload out of `routingCtx.ReqBody` while it routes, so a rewrite that waited for the target pod would leave the prefill leg, the heavy one, at the engine default. Applying before routing gives both legs the field from a single edit;
  - the forwarded body is then the only body, so there is no second copy to keep in sync and no content-length rule per dispatch path.
- One behavior change to call out on the delegated path: `RouterNotSet` now sets `content-length` where it previously set only `model`. The response replaces the upstream body with `routingCtx.ReqBody`, and the size is what Envoy validates the upstream request against, so the header describes the body that is actually forwarded. While the opt-in is off the body is untouched and the value matches the length that would have been sent anyway; it becomes load bearing only once a tier is mapped. Setting it conditionally would bring back the per-path branch this change removes.
- `cmd/plugins/main.go` reads the new environment variable, defaulting to `false`.

### Test Plan

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...`, `staticcheck -checks='QF*'` on the gateway and plugin packages, a focused `-race` run, and a `sphinx-build -W --keep-going` pass are all clean.
- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/types/... ./cmd/...` passes.
- New tests in `gateway_req_priority_test.go` cover the tier lookup (case-insensitive, unknown, empty, whitespace-only), the injection rules on the routing context alone (opt-out byte for byte, unmapped tier, caller-set `priority` including `0`, and the non-object bodies: array, empty, `null`, JSON string, truncated), and the end-to-end handler in both dispatch modes: routed and unrouted, with and without a mapped tier, each asserting the `content-length` header matches the forwarded body. Removing the `RouterNotSet` content-length line makes the two unrouted cases fail, so that part of the change is pinned rather than incidental.
- `TestHandleRequestBody_PriorityTierBeforeRouting` captures the routing context inside `Route` and asserts the priority is already in the body the router sees, and that the forwarded body is the same one. This is the PD prefill guarantee, and it needs two ready pods: a single ready pod takes the pinned-pod fast path in `selectTargetPod` that never calls the router.
- `TestHandleRequestHeaders_PriorityTierIsTrimmed` pins that the header value is trimmed when it is recorded, which is where the tier lookup expects that to happen.
- `gateway_req_body_test.go` asserts the exact header set of an unrouted request, now including `content-length: 74` for a 74-byte body, which is what pins the opt-out path as byte-for-byte.

### Notes

- `docs/source/features/gateway-plugins.rst` and `pkg/plugins/gateway/ENV_VARS.md` were also touched by #2786, which merged after this branch was cut. The additions here sit away from that change's hunks (a new section before **Headers Reference** and one table row at the end of **Target and General Headers**), and the PR still merges cleanly against the current base.

Refs #2286

title: [Feat] Drive gateway routing thresholds from model config profiles
body:
## Pull Request Description

#1961 asks for the gateway plugin configuration to move onto routing profiles, split into what needs backward compatibility and what does not. This PR moves the per-request routing thresholds a model config profile (`model.aibrix.ai/config`) can select for its own requests into `routingConfig` (plus the model-level `ttftThresholdS`), with the environment as the fallback default: a deployment without these fields routes exactly as before.

**Review guide**

- One funnel: `ResolveRoutingOverrides` in `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/profile_knobs.go` runs once per request inside `Server.selectTargetPod` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway.go`), so every strategy downstream reads the same resolved values from the routing context.
- Core logic beyond the resolver: `pkg/plugins/gateway/configprofiles/configprofiles.go` (profile loading). Consumers: `algorithms/pd/*`, `algorithms/vtc/*`, `load_balance.go`, `router.go`, `prefix_cache*.go`, `gateway_rsp_body.go`.
- Fallback: environment values stay the process default (`algorithms/pd/env_overrides.go`, `algorithms/vtc/env_overrides.go`); a profile field wins only when the profile sets it.
- Mechanical: type definitions in `pkg/types/*`, plus tests (24 of the 51 files) and docs (three `.rst` files and `ENV_VARS.md`).

**What moves into the profile**

- `ttftThresholdS` (top level, next to `routingStrategy`): overrides `AIBRIX_TTFT_THRESHOLD_S` for the profile's first-token-delay classification.
- `routingConfig.pd.*`: the decode abort timeout and retry delay, the four imbalance spread thresholds, the decode load-balance weights, the token-load charge knobs, `hybridCacheLoadFactor`, `minMatchPct` and `prefillRequestTimeout`.
- `routingConfig.promptLengthBucketing` (flat, next to `promptLenBucket*`), `routingConfig.loadBalance.*`, `routingConfig.prefixCache.standardDeviationFactor`, `routingConfig.preble.targetGPU` and `decodingLength`, `routingConfig.vtc.*`, and `routingConfig.autoBlend.*`.

**Compatibility and semantics**

- Every knob keeps its matching `AIBRIX_*` variable as the default. A knob the profile leaves unset, or sets to a value the variable would reject (a negative factor, a percentage outside its range, an unknown GPU name), is dropped at the profile boundary, so a profile can only narrow or sharpen routing behavior and a deployment without these fields routes exactly as before.
- Knobs that configure process-wide state stay environment-only on purpose, because all models of one gateway process share that state: the preble histogram window and eviction loop, the VTC token tracker window, time unit and token floors plus its input/output token weights, the session-affinity local cache capacity, and the router string cache bound. The docs list them explicitly.
- Deployment-level settings (tokenizer endpoints, Redis and statesync settings, the rate limiting switches, `AIBRIX_KV_CONNECTOR_TYPE`) also stay environment-only, as before.
- The knobs are resolved once per request. The non-PD path parks them on the `RoutingContext`, and `reset` clears them so a pooled context cannot leak the previous request's thresholds into a request whose profile sets none. The PD path parks them on the `PDLegState`, because the async prefill goroutine and the decode abort outlive the client stream and must not read a recycled routing context.

**Docs**

`gateway-plugins.rst` gains a per-request routing knobs table (field, overridden variable, description) and the environment-only list; `ENV_VARS.md` gains a variable-to-field mapping section; the PD and model-deployment pages point at the new section.

## Test Plan

title: [CI] Cancel superseded pull-request workflow runs
body:
## Pull Request Description

Superseded runs stay in the queue and keep holding runners while the newest push waits behind them.

Measured on 2026-09-22 (UTC) in this repository:

- At 07:39Z, 31 workflow runs were queued or in progress, and 12 of them were already at a commit that is no longer the head of its pull request. One of those had been waiting since 03:17Z.
- Queue time dominates the wall clock. Sampled `Linter and Unit Tests` runs waited 38 minutes to 2 hours 35 minutes for their first job, while the jobs themselves run in 2 to 9 minutes.
- A pull request pushed at 06:56Z had 19 checks. Its first job started 30 minutes later, and the remaining checks were still queued 45 minutes after the push.

Changes:

- Add a `concurrency` group to the workflows that run on pull requests. The group is keyed on the pull request number, so a newer push cancels the run it supersedes. `push` and `workflow_dispatch` runs fall back to a per-run group, so their behavior is unchanged. The triage bot uses the issue or pull request number.
- Add `timeout-minutes` to jobs that did not set one. The default is 360 minutes, so a job that hangs can hold a runner for six hours. The values stay well above the observed runtimes. The longest job, `Installation E2E Tests`, already takes about 41 minutes and is capped at 75.

Nothing changes about what is verified: the checks that gate a pull request always run for its current head. Cancel-in-progress only drops runs for commits that a newer push has already replaced.

## Pull Request Description Replace the request drain-rate capacity in the load-balance router with score = (running + λ·queued) / EWMA(output tokens/sec) × (1 + α·(1 − kvFree)²) and route to the lowest score. Capacity (observed token throughput), load (committed work) and KV headroom are now separate inputs, so a saturated replica is no longer read as "send it more traffic" and request size no longer skews the capacity estimate on heterogeneous hardware. - Cache: count output tokens completed per pod (gateway-tracked, engine agnostic, carried across pod delete/re-add like completedRequests) and publish RealtimeOutputTokenRateEWMA: the 1-minute token rate smoothed with a 10s time constant. title: [Misc] Add queue observability metrics to the gateway SLO queue
body:
## Pull Request Description

The gateway's SLO queue (`routingAlgorithm=slo`) is invisible on the metrics surface: nothing reports how long a request waits for a slot, how deep the queue runs, how requests leave it, or whether the queue is serving FIFO because no profile was usable. This adds four metrics around the queue, emitted from the request path itself:

| Metric | Type | Extra label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gateway_queue_wait_time_bucket_total` | Counter | `bucket` | Time from enqueue to leaving the queue |
| `gateway_queue_pending_requests` | Gauge | - | Current queue depth for the model |
| `gateway_queue_outcome_total` | Counter | `outcome` | How the request left: `routed`, `slo_failure`, `capacity_reached`, `error` |
| `gateway_queue_fifo_fallback_total` | Counter | `reason` | Dispatches served by the FIFO fallback: `no_profile`, `no_slo_info` |

Wait time is stamped on the routing context when the request is enqueued (`RoutingContext.QueueStartTime`), so the bucket measures residency in the queue rather than time since arrival; a context that was never stamped falls back to `RequestTime`. The bucket bounds (10ms to 60s) are coarser than the request-path duration buckets because a request can wait tens of seconds for capacity, and they follow the existing label convention (`low-highms`, `Nms+`) instead of introducing a histogram.

`outcome` is classified with `errors.Is`, so wrapped errors still land in the right bucket: `ErrorSLOFailureRequest` -> `slo_failure`, `ErrorLoadCapacityReached` -> `capacity_reached`, anything else -> `error`. The FIFO fallback is recorded where the decision is made: `SLOQueue.Peek` marks the fallback candidate with its reason and `Dequeue` counts it once.

All four are emitted with the same low-cardinality label set as the other gateway request metrics (`model`, `lora_adapter`, `gateway_pod`) and never with pod labels, keeping the cardinality direction discussed in #2569; the pod that serves the request is already covered by the per-pod request metrics. Pending depth is set (`Set(Len())`) after enqueue and after dequeue rather than incremented and decremented, so an error between the two cannot drift the gauge.

Tests: `TestQueueWaitBucketLabel` pins the bucket bounds, `TestQueueOutcomeLabel` pins the four outcomes (including a wrapped error), `TestQueueMetricsRegistered` guards against a metric being dropped silently because it is missing from the registry, and `TestQueueRouterEmitsQueueMetricsByOutcome` drives a `queueRouter` end to end with a fake queue and backend for the four outcomes, checking the emitted labels and the pending sequence `1 -> 0`. The SLOQueue fallback reasons are covered by two ginkgo specs plus a ranked-candidate control case.

`gofmt` and `go vet` are clean; `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/types/... ./pkg/metrics/...` and `go test -race` on the two touched packages pass.

## Related Issues

Related to: #2569 (low-cardinality direction for gateway metrics).

title: [Feat] Recover panics on the gateway plugin request path
body:
## Pull Request Description

The plugin had no panic recovery on the ExtProc path: `grpc.NewServer` in `cmd/plugins/main.go` is built with the OTel stats handler and a max message size and nothing else, so one panic in the stream handler ends the whole `aibrix-gateway-plugins` process together with every request in flight on it. #2756 hit exactly that on the routing path (a malformed profile making `ModelGPUProfile.GetSignature` panic); #1284 (index out of range in the queue) and #2049 (pod restarts under high concurrency) have the same blast radius on the same path.

This recovers at the server boundary, with no new dependency:

```go
opts = append(opts, grpc.StreamInterceptor(gateway.StreamPanicRecoveryInterceptor()))
```

A recovered panic logs the stack trace, counts a new `gateway_request_panic_total` counter, and fails only the stream it happened on with `codes.Internal`. The panic value stays in the log and the reply only names the method, the way other internal errors on the request path are reported.

Both questions from the issue are answered by the change: the stream interceptor is the primary home because it covers every handler on that server, and the `Process` defer stays as the fallback for callers that never go through the transport. The metric follows the existing gateway naming, pod-scoped with the `pod_name` label, since no constraint was recorded. A handler error is passed through unchanged rather than being rewritten as a panic.

Verified by:
- a real gRPC server with the interceptor registered: the stream whose handler panics ends with `codes.Internal`, and a second stream on the same server still runs;
- reverting the interceptor locally: the same test dies with the raw `panic: boom in Process`, which is the blast radius this PR removes;
- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/metrics/...`, `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/ ./pkg/metrics/`, `go vet` and `gofmt` clean.

Recovery is a last line of defense, not a replacement for fixing the defect, and it cannot catch runtime-fatal conditions such as concurrent map writes or OOM.

title: fix(kvcache): decode vLLM map-format KV events; tier-aware prefix scoring
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2285. While investigating, I found a larger compatibility break:
vLLM switched KV event encoding from positional arrays to **msgpack maps** in
[vllm-project/vllm#42892](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42892)
(merged 2026-06-09). `DecodeEventBatch` still expected `[ts, events]` arrays,
so **every** KV event payload from current vLLM fails to unmarshal
(`msgpack: invalid code=0x88 decoding array length`) — kv-events prefix
routing is effectively dead against current vLLM. The legacy publisher also
sent one event per ZMQ message (tag-first array), which the batch-shaped
decoder never handled either.

## Changes

- `pkg/cache/kvcache/msgpack_decoder.go`: accept all three wire shapes —
  map single event (current vLLM), tag-first array single event (legacy
  vLLM), and `[ts, events]` batch (older code paths / test encoder).
- Parse every `BlockStored`/`BlockRemoved` field: `lora_id`, `medium`,
  `lora_name`, `extra_keys`, `group_idx`, `kv_cache_spec_kind`,
  `kv_cache_spec_sliding_window`, `locality`.
- `pkg/utils/syncprefixcacheindexer`: record the storage `medium` per
  (prefix, pod) and weight `MatchPrefix` scores (GPU=1.0, CPU=0.5,
  STORAGE=0.25; unspecified keeps full score for backward compatibility)
  so pods holding a prefix only on a slower tier are not over-credited.
- Plumb `medium`/`lora_name`/`group_idx` through the `kvevent` handler and
  `store_providers` adapter (previously dropped at the handler).

## Tests

New `decoder_vllm_compat_test.go` verifies decoding against **byte-exact
payloads generated with the real msgspec encoder** for both current map and
legacy array formats (single-event and batch shapes). New
`medium_scoring_test.go` covers tier weighting via `AddPrefixWithMedium` and
the event ingestion path. All existing `kvcache` and
`syncprefixcacheindexer` tests keep passing.

## Follow-up

The `(model, lora_name, group_idx)` index keying part of #2285 needs a
request-side adapter id (`RoutingContext` has no LoRA field today); see the
issue thread.

title: [Bug] Gate the session-affinity Redis refresh on the stored value
body:
## Pull Request Description

The Redis write-through for session-key pinning still refreshed with an unconditional `SET`: a TTL refresh for an old address that landed after another replica had repinned the session silently wrote the old address back, reverting the newer pinning, and it also pushed out the TTL of whatever value was stored by the time it ran.

This gates the refresh on the stored value through a small Lua script that compares and writes in one atomic step:

```go
var sessionKeyRefreshScript = redis.NewScript(`
local current = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
if not current then
  redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'PX', tonumber(ARGV[2]))
  return {2}
end
if current == ARGV[1] then
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[2]))
  return {1}
end
return {0, current}
`)
```

The TTL is extended when the stored value still matches `addr`, the pin is re-attached with a fresh TTL when the key is missing (so an actively used session cannot lose its affinity right at the expiry boundary, and nothing can be overwritten), and nothing is written when the key holds a different address. On that mismatch the script returns the stored value with the outcome, so the refresh converges the local entry on the exact value that rejected it, without a second read that could miss a key expiring in between, even a confirmed entry, since the refresh just established that Redis no longer vouches for it, the same way a lost claim already converges; the stale replica therefore follows the newer pin instead of routing from the old address until the next sync pass. A Lua script rather than GET followed by SET/EXPIRE is used because the gate has to hold against concurrent writers; it goes through `redis.NewScript`, so refreshes on the hot path run by EVALSHA once the server has it cached, matching the pattern already used for the gateway's async-job scripts. A reply the script cannot emit is treated as a failure rather than a confirmation. Failover repins keep the unconditional write; their compare-and-swap is the remaining follow-up recorded in the TODO.

This is the refresh half of the write-semantics feedback from the #2742 review (discussion_r4037407790), split out after the claim half (#2765) merged. Say the word if you would rather see the remaining repin CAS folded in here instead.

Verified by reverting the fix locally: with the gated refresh replaced by the plain SET, the new regression spec fails with `10.0.0.1:8000` reappearing over the repinned `10.0.0.2:8000` and its TTL being extended; with the fix it passes. `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, and `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/utils/...` all pass.

## Related Issues

title: [Bug] Purge a pod's prefix cache when the engine sleep-state metric shows it went to sleep
body:
Closes #2287.

This grew from what it started as. Original scope was just the metric label-filtering bug below; the tracker and edge-triggered purge (the actual backstop) turned out to be ready sooner than the original PR description said to expect, so it's in the same PR now rather than a follow-up.

## The bug this fixes

`vllm:engine_sleep_state` reports one gauge family with three instances per pod, distinguished only by the `sleep_state` label (`awake`, `weights_offloaded`, `discard_all`), each its own 0/1 series. Nothing in the Prometheus exposition format guarantees scrape order, but `parseMetricFromFamily` read `metricFamily.Metric[0]` unconditionally, so which of the three series aibrix actually recorded depended on whatever order that particular scrape happened to return.

Added `Metric.RequiredLabelKey`/`RequiredLabelValue`: when set, `parseMetricFromFamily` searches the family for the instance whose label matches instead of taking the first one. Every other registered metric leaves this unset and keeps the exact `Metric[0]` behavior it has today. `EngineSleepState` now filters to `sleep_state=awake`.

## The backstop

The `AllBlocksCleared` ZMQ event handler already purges a pod's prefix cache on `/reset_prefix_cache`, OOM-driven reset, or `/sleep`. It's not complete: vLLM only flushes queued KV events from inside a scheduler step, so an idle or sleeping engine may never emit one, and ZMQ delivery is lossy. The pod stays `Running` with `/health` returning 200, so the prefix router keeps preferring it for prefixes whose blocks are gone.

`Manager.CheckSleepStateBackstop` reads the (now correctly filtered) `engine_sleep_state` value already scraped every refresh tick and purges on the awake-to-asleep transition, per (pod, model). Edge triggered, not level triggered: `RemovePrefix` takes the prefix router's write lock and is O(P) in cached prefixes for the model, so purging on every tick a sleeping pod is observed would hold that lock once per refresh interval for as long as it stays asleep. A (pod, model) pair with no prior observation is seeded as having been awake, so a gateway restart while a pod is already asleep still self-corrects on the first observation.

`Manager.PurgePodPrefixCache` factors the get-indexer-then-`RemovePrefix` logic the event handler already had into a method the backstop also calls, so a pod's cache is purged the same way whether aibrix learned about it from a ZMQ event or from this metric. `unsubscribeFromPod` now also forgets the pod's tracked sleep state, so a reused pod key is seeded fresh.

Wired into `pkg/cache`'s existing `worker()` metrics loop, right where `engine_sleep_state` is already read for Prometheus export. No new scraping. `KVEventManager.CheckSleepStateBackstop` is a no-op in the default (non-zmq) build, matching every other `KVEventManager` method: the backstop needs the sync indexer KV event sync provides.

title: [Bug] Use SET NX for the initial session-affinity Redis claim
body:
## Pull Request Description

The Redis write-through for session-key pinning shares one unconditional `SET` across three cases with different concurrency-safety needs: the initial claim, TTL-only refreshes, and failover repins. That leaves the initial claim racy: two gateway replicas that both miss Redis and resolve different pods for the same session can overwrite each other's pinning (last writer wins), and an unconfirmed sync-pass retry can replace a pinning that another replica already owns.

This makes the claim atomic instead: `persistSessionKeyToRedis` now takes the caller's write intent, and the claim persists with `SET NX EX`:

```go
if mode == writeClaim {
	claimed, err := r.redisClient.SetNX(ctx, sessionAffinityRedisKey(cacheKey), addr, sessionAffinityTTL).Result()
	if err != nil {
		klog.V(4).ErrorS(err, "failed to persist session key pinning to redis", "cache_key", cacheKey)
		return false
	}
	if !claimed {
		return false
	}
	r.markSessionKeyConfirmed(cacheKey, addr)
	return true
}
```

A fresh rendezvous pick on the route path, the sync-pass retry, an unconfirmed local-cache hit, and the post-route commit (the single-ready-pod fast path and blended commits) all use this claim mode. A lost claim reads the winner back and converges the local entry on it, so the losing replica follows the winner on its next request instead of waiting for the sync pass. Refresh and repin intentionally keep the unconditional write for now. Gating a refresh on the stored value still matching `addr` (so a delayed refresh cannot revert a newer repin) and a compare-and-swap for repins are the follow-ups recorded in the TODO at the call site, and the write-intent plumbing added here is what those build on. Say the word if you would rather see those folded into a single larger change instead.

Verified by reverting each part of the fix locally: the added specs fail with the losing replica's address replacing the existing pinning (`10.0.0.2:8000` landing over `10.0.0.1:8000`), and pass with the fix. `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, and `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/cache/...` all pass.

body:
## Pull Request Description Adds Redis-backed session-key pinning so `session-affinity` can keep concurrent agentic requests on the same inference pod across gateway replicas, plus follow-up correctness fixes so that stickiness actually holds after scale-out, cache isolation, and blend behavior. ### Agentic routing `x-session-id` only works after the first response comes back, which is too late for agentic workloads that fan out concurrent tool calls or sub-agent requests. Callers can now send a stable `x-aibrix-session-key` from the first request: - Sequential multi-turn chat still uses the gateway-issued `x-session-id`. - Concurrent/agentic requests use a caller-owned `x-aibrix-session-key` (conversation ID, agent-run ID, etc.). - With `REDIS_HOST` configured, the key→pod pinning is shared across gateway replicas (1-hour sliding TTL). Without Redis, mapping stays deterministic via rendezvous hashing over the current ready pod set. - Keys longer than 256 bytes are treated as unset and fall back to normal session-affinity resolution. - The same header can be reused by PD `token_load` / `hybrid_cache_load` policies. Docs: `docs/source/features/agentic-routing.rst`. ### Correctness Follow-ups - **Drop the session-affinity load-balance auto-blend:** Session-affinity `ScoreAll` is binary (1 for the resolved pod, 0 elsewhere), so the previous 5:4 blend could never be overridden by load-balance disagreement. Bare `session-affinity` now runs unblended, like `pd` / `slo*` / standalone `load-balance`. Prefix-cache keeps the 5:4 ratio because its scoring is graded. - **Honor stickiness on the single-ready-pod fast path:** `selectTargetPod` used to return that pod without calling `router.Route()`, so a session started while only one pod was ready never got a Redis pin or `x-session-id` header. After scale-out, rendezvous hashing could move the session. The router's `PostRouteUpdate` hook now runs on that path, including through `multiStrategyRouter`. - **Isolate and bound the session-key cache:** Redis/local cache keys are scoped by model (`sessionCacheKey`) so two models sharing Redis — or a reused session-key value — don't overwrite each other. The local `sessionKeyPods` cache is capped by `AIBRIX_SESSION_AFFINITY_MAX_LOCAL_KEYS` (default 100k); past the cap, new keys still resolve via Redis or rendezvous hashing. - **Harden Lookup / local-cache races:** `Lookup` rejects a nil provider instead of dereferencing it. `storeSessionKeyLocal` uses a `LoadOrStore` / `CompareAndSwap` retry loop so concurrent writes can't clobber a newer pinning or un-confirm one whose Redis write already landed. > **Note / Known Leftover:** `persistSessionKeyToRedis`'s unconditional `SET` is shared by initial-claim, TTL-refresh, and failover-repin writes and can still race across gateway replicas. title: [Bug] Keep ranked candidates in SLOQueue when a rank lookup fails
body:
## Pull Request Description

One failed profile ranking made `SLOQueue.Peek` drop every ranked candidate and serve the earliest request in FIFO order. The rank error was stored in a variable shared by the whole scan, and after the scan the candidate list was truncated to the first (FIFO fallback) entry; a profile that cannot rank a single request, for example one whose index table does not cover the request signature, therefore collapsed the routing decision for all subqueues.

`rankImpl` already reports per-profile errors and `Peek` logs a warning for them, so this finishes that contract:

```go
if rankErr != nil {
	klog.Warningf("SLOQueue failed to get SLO info for request %s with profile %s: %v, skip.", r.RequestID, profile.Deployment, rankErr)
	continue
}
```

Candidates whose profiles all fail are removed from the ranked list instead of taking part in the cross-candidate sort. A subqueue with no rankable profiles still falls back to FIFO; I left that path unchanged, so say the word if you would rather revisit it.

title: [Gateway] Fail the client request and abort the decode leg when the SGLang PD prefill leg fails
body:
## Pull Request Description In SGLang PD disaggregation the gateway fires the prefill leg asynchronously and lets Envoy forward the decode leg. When the prefill leg fails (dead prefill pod, non-2xx, timeout, client cancel) nothing tells the decode pod or the client: the decode pod sits in its bootstrap / prealloc queue for that `bootstrap_room` until the engine's own bootstrap timeout (minutes), holding a decode slot, and the client sees a long hang followed by an opaque decode-side error. This is #2289. This PR keeps the prefill dispatch asynchronous (the constraint raised in #2289) and only stops discarding its result. ### What changes 1. **`utils.LoadEnvNonNegativeInt`** — `LoadEnvInt` treats every value ≤ 0 as invalid and silently falls back, so a knob whose documented value `0` means "off" cannot be switched off from the environment. The new helper accepts 0 and still refuses negative/unparseable values. `LoadEnvInt` is unchanged for its callers. 2. **Gateway-owned `rid` + decode abort on prefill failure.** SGLang's `/abort_request` matches on `rid` only (`AbortReq` has no room field) and reads `rid` from the request body, not from `X-Request-Id`. The gateway now writes `rid = -<16-hex nonce>` into both legs' bodies (fixed width because SGLang's abort match is prefix based; the nonce keeps retries with a reused request id distinct). When the async prefill leg fails, the failure is classified (`http_status`, `timeout`, `canceled`, `transport`, `request_setup`, `bad_response`) and the gateway POSTs `{"rid": ...}` to the decode pod's `/abort_request`. The abort is best-effort on its own goroutine with its own timeout, sent twice (immediately and after a short delay) because a prefill pod that refuses the connection outright lets the first abort overtake the decode leg, and the tokenizer manager silently drops an abort for an unknown rid. It is skipped once the decode pod has started responding. `bad_response` (HTTP 200 with an unparseable body) never aborts because the transfer did complete. 3. **Fail the client request immediately.** `Route()` only produces the header mutation, but the same ext_proc stream stays open for the response and is parked in `srv.Recv()` waiting for decode response headers that will not arrive until the bootstrap timeout. `srv.Recv()` moves into one reader goroutine per stream and the processing loop becomes a `select` over the reader, the stream context and a per-request prefill-failure wakeup. Non-PD streams select on exactly the two cases they had before. When a terminal prefill failure lands before the decode pod has responded, the gateway answers with an `ImmediateResponse` (503 for timeout/transport/request_setup/canceled, the upstream status for `http_status`, 502 otherwise) carrying an OpenAI-shaped error body and `x-error-pd-prefill: true`, then closes the stream with a gRPC error so `failure_mode_allow: false` makes Envoy reset the decode connection. If the decode pod has already responded, the failure is only recorded. The per-request leg state lives in a per-incarnation object captured by the prefill goroutine before launch, so a late prefill failure can never land on a recycled `RoutingContext` that another request has since taken from the pool (there is a test seam that reproduces the aliasing deterministically). 4. **Observability.** `gateway_pd_prefill_failure_total{class,stage}` (`stage` = `before_response` / `after_response`), `gateway_pd_decode_abort_total{prefill_failure_class,result}`, structured log lines `pd_prefill_fail_fast` and `pd_decode_abort`. The generic request-fail counters carry `status="pd_prefill_failure"` so a fail-fast is separable from an upstream 503. A fail-fast runs `finalizeRouterContext` exactly once and is never counted as a successful request. 5. **Env vars** (documented in `pkg/plugins/gateway/ENV_VARS.md`): `AIBRIX_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (existing), `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_TIMEOUT` (seconds, default 3, `0` disables the abort), `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_RETRY_DELAY` (seconds, default 2, `0` sends a single attempt). 6. **Tests.** Unit tests for the failure classification, the abort scheduling (both attempts, skip-after-response, `0` semantics), the `select` and the fail-fast response, plus a regression test for the pooled-context aliasing. e2e (`test/e2e/gateway/pd/pd_fail_fast_test.go`): `TestPDPrefillFailFastRejectedPrefill` rejects the prefill leg with the mock while holding the decode leg for 10 s (new role-scoped `x-aibrix-mock-delay-role` header on the mock app) and asserts the client is answered with the prefill status + `x-error-pd-prefill: true` before the decode leg could respond, and that a decode mock recorded `/abort_request` with the gateway's rid; `TestPDPrefillFailFastPrefillTimeout` covers the `timeout` class / 503 mapping and skips itself unless the gateway is deployed with a short `AIBRIX_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (exported as `AIBRIX_E2E_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), because the shipped 60 s exceeds the mock's delay cap. The mock app gains an `/abort_request` route so the abort is observable. ### Notes for review - Commits are separable: (1) `LoadEnvNonNegativeInt`, (2) rid + decode abort, (3) client fail-fast, (4) e2e + docs. Each builds and vets on its own. - `http_status` passes the prefill engine's own 4xx/5xx through to the client (502 if it is not a code Envoy names); the other classes map to 503. Happy to switch to "always 503 with the upstream status in the body" if preferred. - `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_TIMEOUT=0` is the off switch for the abort. A dedicated boolean would work as well; this keeps the knob count down. - `TestPDFailureSGLangAsyncPrefillHandoff` now normally sees the gateway's fail-fast response before the decode mock's own 500; its `>= 500` assertion still holds and the decode mock still records its handoff failure. Flagging it in case it flakes on CI. - Race detector is clean on `pkg/plugins/gateway`, `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/...` and `pkg/types`; `make lint` and `make licensecheck` pass. ### Verification on a real deployment Fault injection on a 2-prefill / 2-decode SGLang deployment with a gateway built from the equivalent change, prefill request timeout set to 3 s so that a cold ~24k-token prompt times out on the prefill leg: | scenario | client | decode pod | prefill pod | |---|---|---|---| | prefill timeout, abort enabled | 6/6 got 503 at 3.01 s (before: hang until the engine's 300–600 s bootstrap timeout) | `AbortReq` dequeued + ACKed 6/6, prealloc/transfer queues back to baseline | abort notification in the same second, 6/6 released | | prefill timeout, `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_TIMEOUT=0` | same 503 at 3.01 s | released by the Envoy reset alone ≈1.1 s after the 503 | ≈1.1 s after the 503 | | `kill -9` a prefill pod under load | requests on the dead pod: 503 in 2.2 s (`transport`); requests on the healthy pod: 200 | abort ACKed 4/4 | n/a | No collateral under normal load (≈1,800 requests, ≈65k-token prompts, no injected failures): every abort attempt logged was the "client closed the stream after completion" echo, all after the request's own `request_end` (Δ 0.1–0.6 ms), all skipped because the decode pod had already responded; the engines' `num_aborted_requests_total` did not move on any pod. Routing overhead: `routing_time` p50 5.4 ms, p99 81 → 185 ms. ## Related Issues Resolves: #2289

title: [Bug] Guard ModelGPUProfile.GetSignature against short indexes
body:
## Pull Request Description

`ModelGPUProfile.GetSignature` reads `indexes[i]` once per requested feature but only checks the inner slices, so a profile with fewer index ranges than features (a missing `indexes` field unmarshals to nil) panics with `index out of range`. The gRPC server in `cmd/plugins/main.go` is built without a recovery interceptor, so one malformed profile terminates the plugin process instead of failing a single routing decision.

The Python estimator already treats any dimension mismatch as an error: `get_signature()` raises before doing any work. This adds the equivalent guard on the Go side:

```go
if len(indexes) != len(features) {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("profile index size mismatch, got %d, expected %d", len(indexes), len(features))
}
ret := make([]int, len(features))
```

`rankImpl` propagates `GetSignature` errors and `Peek` logs a warning and skips the profile, so the failure becomes "this deployment was not scored" and the gateway stays up. The guard requires an exact match, so profiles with extra index ranges are rejected as well instead of producing a short signature that fails later in `getValue`.

Verified by reverting the guard locally: the short-index specs fail with `index out of range`, while the extra-index case silently returns a short signature; with the guard, `go test ./pkg/cache/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/...` passes.

The cache already maintains a cross-gateway running-request count for every routed request, exposed through Cache.GetPodsRunningRequests, and least-request reads it. Read it from there instead. Route now samples two distinct ready pods, reads both counts in a single GetPodsRunningRequests call, and routes to the lower one. For pods that serve several ports, the port is chosen with the same helper least-request uses. The router keeps no state of its own, so the Redis client, key rotation, tracker hooks and lastRoutingTime are gone, and power-of-two registers via init() like the other routers instead of requiring Redis (RegisterPowerOfTwoRouter and NewPowerOfTwoRouterWithRedis are removed). The per-port metric the cache exposes holds the pod's total running count rather than a per-port count, so port choice for data-parallel pods is only approximately load-aware, as it already is for least-request. title: [Bug] Skip profile cache updates when Redis client is nil in standalo…
body:
The gateway-plugin panics with a nil pointer dereference **~10 seconds after startup** in standalone mode without Redis, which contradicts the documented behavior
  (`deployment/local/README.md`: *"Redis is not required in local mode. Without Redis, rate limiting is disabled but routing works normally."*).

  **Panic:**

  ```
  panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

  goroutine 114 [running]:
  github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/cache.(*Store).updateDeploymentProfiles(...)
      pkg/cache/cache_profile.go:36
  github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/cache.initProfileCache.func1()
      pkg/cache/cache_init.go:553
  created by github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg.cache.initProfileCache in goroutine 1
      pkg/cache/cache_init.go:548
  ```

  **Root cause:** `initProfileCache` unconditionally starts the 10s profile-refresh ticker, and on the first tick `updateDeploymentProfiles` calls `c.redisClient.Scan(...)` at
  `pkg/cache/cache_profile.go:36` without a nil check. In standalone mode with no Redis, `main()` deliberately continues with a nil `RedisClient` (warning: *"Running without
  Redis: rate limiting and user auth disabled"*), and `InitOptions.RedisClient` is documented as "Can be nil" — every sibling initializer in `cache_init.go` guards with `if
  opts.RedisClient != nil` (lines 420/425/432) except this one. Regression introduced in #1192 (`cf64e51b`).

  **Fix:** Skip the background refresh loop in `initProfileCache` when `store.redisClient` is nil, logging a warning. Two deliberate choices:

  1. `store.pendingLoadProvider = newPendingLoadProvider(store)` stays **unconditional** — it is consumed by the request-tracing path (`cache_trace.go:355`) independently of
  Redis and must not be disabled by this fix.
  2. The guard is placed inside `initProfileCache` (not at the call site) so the semantics of `enableProfileCaching` ("is the profile feature wanted") remain decoupled from
  Redis availability. Consumers already degrade gracefully when profiles are absent: `GetModelProfileByPod` returns `MissingProfileError`, and `cache_trace.go:372` explicitly
  treats it as non-fatal.

  **Workaround (verified on unpatched binary):** setting `AIBRIX_MODEL_GPU_PROFILE_CACHING_FLAG=false` also avoids the panic, confirming the profile-refresh path is the only
  crash source.

  **Testing:**

  - `go build ./pkg/cache/` and `go vet ./pkg/cache/` pass; `go test ./pkg/cache/` passes.
  - End-to-end on macOS (built `gateway-plugins` with `-tags "nozmq"` from `main` @ `abb2cd20`): standalone mode + `--endpoints-config` + **no Redis running** → unpatched binary
   crashes after the first 10s tick; patched binary stays alive and logs `"Redis client is nil, skipping deployment profile cache updates"` (observed process alive >13s).

  **Open question for maintainers (out of scope here):** in Kubernetes mode, a misconfigured Redis now silently disables profile-based features. A fail-fast at startup (similar
  to `EnableKVSync`'s `klog.Fatalf` at `cache_init.go:439`) could make such misconfiguration visible, but that changes existing behavior and likely deserves its own discussion.

  ## Related Issues

  Resolves: #2754

title: [API] Reject StormService /scale above 1 in Pooled mode
body:
## Pull Request Description

#2450 and #2617 added optional `StormServiceSpec.Mode` and consume it in the controller and PodAutoscaler. Create/update admission already rejects a declared `mode: Pooled` with `spec.replicas > 1`.

That check does not run for the `/scale` subresource. `kubectl scale`, HPA, and other external autoscalers write `spec.replicas` through `/scale`, so a pooled StormService could still be scaled above one RoleSet.

This change registers a validating webhook for `stormservices/scale`. The handler loads the parent StormService, applies the proposed replica count, and reuses `validateStormServiceMode`:

- Declared `mode: Pooled` cannot set replicas > 1 via `/scale`. The admission error tells operators to scale roles through `spec.template.spec.roles[].replicas` instead.
- Declared `mode: Replica` can still scale `spec.replicas`.
- Omitted `spec.mode` is not pinned to inferred Pooled, so existing replica scaling continues to work.

Helm and kubebuilder webhook manifests include the new `vstormservicescale.kb.io` rule.

### Tests

- Unit: reject/allow table for `/scale` (Pooled > 1, Pooled == 1, Replica > 1, omitted mode > 1), plus malformed Scale and missing StormService.
- Integration: envtest `/scale` subresource reject for declared Pooled, allow for declared Replica, allow when mode is omitted.

Verified locally:

```
go test -count=1 ./pkg/webhook/
ok  	github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/webhook	0.089s

make test-integration-webhook
Ran 84 of 84 Specs in 7.265 seconds
SUCCESS! -- 84 Passed | 0 Failed
```

## Related Issues
Part of #2449. This is the leftover `/scale` subresource enforcement from the follow-up list after #2450 and #2617. It does not close #2449; the original issue still has remaining items such as reporting the resolved mode in status.

title: feat: add Valkey as OSS metadata store option with external managed endpoint support
body:
## Pull Request Description

Adds [Valkey](https://valkey.io/) (Linux Foundation, BSD-3 licensed) as an OSS-licensed
alternative to Redis for the AIBrix metadata store, and wires the existing
`ExternalConnectionConfig` API so operators can point the KV-cache controller at a managed
Valkey/Redis-compatible endpoint (e.g., Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey) instead of an
in-cluster pod.

All changes are purely additive and backward-compatible. Existing Redis configuration is
untouched and remains the default.

### Why

Redis 7.x ships under RSALv2/SSPLv1 (not OSI-approved). Valkey is a wire-compatible fork
under BSD-3. The existing `go-redis` client and all `REDIS_*` env vars work unchanged over
the RESP protocol. This unblocks deployments where open-source license compliance is required.

The `ExternalConnectionConfig` struct already existed in the CRD API — this PR wires it into
the reconcile loop so it is actually functional.

### Changes

**Part 1 — Valkey as a drop-in image option**

- `config/metadata/valkey.yaml` — New K8s Deployment + Service using `valkey/valkey:8-alpine`.
  Service name is `redis-master` so all `REDIS_HOST` references work with no modification.
  Mutually exclusive with `redis.yaml`.
- `deployment/standalone/docker-compose.yml` — Redis image made configurable via `REDIS_IMAGE`
  env var (defaults to `redis:7.4-alpine`). Added `REDIS_SERVER_CMD` / `REDIS_CLI_CMD` for
  healthcheck compatibility with Valkey.
- `hack/release/sync-dependency-images.sh` — Added `valkey/valkey:8` to the release image
  mirror list.
- `deployment/standalone/README.md` — Documented Valkey as an available OSS alternative with
  usage examples.

**Part 2 — ExternalConnectionConfig wiring**

- `pkg/controller/kvcache/backends/distributed.go`:
  - `reconcileRedisService()` now checks `ExternalConnection` first — if set, skips in-cluster
    Redis deployment entirely and cleans up any existing in-cluster Pod/Service during migration
  - Added `validateExternalConnection()` — validates `host:port` format and verifies
    `PasswordSecretRef` secret/key exist (without reading the value)
  - Extracted `parseSecretRef()` and `buildRedisWatcherEnvVars()` — sets `REDIS_ADDR` and
    `REDIS_PASSWORD` via `SecretKeyRef` for both `hpkv` and `infinistore` watchers
  - Added nil-guard for `Runtime` field to prevent panic when only `ExternalConnection` is
    configured
  - Renamed `etcdService` to `metadataService`
- `pkg/controller/kvcache/backends/distributed_test.go` — 5 new subtests covering all
  reconcile paths

### Usage

**Kubernetes — external managed endpoint:**

```yaml
apiVersion: orchestration.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: KVCache
spec:
  metadata:
    redis:
      externalConnection:
        address: "valkey.example.com:6379"
        passwordSecretRef: "valkey-credentials/password"
```

**Kubernetes — Valkey in-cluster** (swap `redis.yaml` for `valkey.yaml` in kustomization.yaml):

```bash
kubectl apply -f config/metadata/valkey.yaml
```

**Docker Compose — Valkey:**

```bash
REDIS_IMAGE=valkey/valkey:8-alpine \
REDIS_SERVER_CMD=valkey-server \
REDIS_CLI_CMD=valkey-cli \
docker compose up -d
```

### Testing

- Part 1: existing integration tests pass (no behavior change to default Redis path)
- Part 2: 5 new unit subtests — skip in-cluster deployment when external connection is set,
  invalid address format, missing password secret, nil Runtime guard, custom secret key format

## Related Issues

Resolves: 

- Wire compatibility confirmed: https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/928

title: [Bug] Fix data race and stale snapshots in utils.Registry
body:
## Pull Request Description

`utils.Registry` caches a slice of its values so `Array()` and `Len()` can serve
readers without taking the lock. The cached slice and its validity flag are two
separate fields, and the lock-free readers load them separately while the writers
replace them under the lock. Three defects follow from that:

**1. The lock-free read is not atomic.** `Array()` (registry.go:110) and `Len()`
(registry.go:145) do `arr, valid := reg.values, reg.valid`. The `// atomic`
comment does not hold: these are two ordinary loads of two independent fields,
racing against the two-value assignments in `Store()` (registry.go:92 and :95)
and `Delete()` (registry.go:63). A reader can observe a truncated `values`
together with a not-yet-cleared `valid`, and return an empty slice for a registry
that was never empty.

**2. A slice already returned to a caller gets rewritten.** The invalidation
branches truncate with `reg.values[:0]` to reuse the backing array, and
`updateArrayLocked()` (registry.go:164) rebuilds into that same array whenever
`cap` is sufficient. `Array()` therefore does not return a snapshot: its contents
change under the caller after any later `Store`/`Delete`. This one reproduces
single-threaded, no race detector involved.

**3. `CustomizedRegistry` has no synchronization at all.** `Store`
(registry.go:101) and `Delete` (registry.go:69) write `reg.values` with no lock
while `Array()` (registry.go:128) reads it with no lock. Worse,
`updateArrayLocked()` publishes `reg.values` while holding the lock and an
unlocked `Store` can clobber it immediately afterwards, so `Array()` can return a
nil `A`. This is the type behind `cache.Model.Pods`.

### Where this happens in production

The writer is the informer callback and the reader is a controller reconcile, in
the same process:

```
write  registry.go:92   <- pkg/cache/informers.go:415  addPodAndModelMappingLocked
                        <- client-go processorListener.run

read   registry.go:110  <- pkg/cache/cache_impl.go:121 ListModelsByPod
                        <- pkg/controller/modeladapter/scheduling/least_adapters.go:43
```

`ListPodsByModel` (cache_impl.go:79) is the same pattern on the gateway request
path, through `CustomizedRegistry`.

The consequences are not only theoretical. `ListModelsByPod` returning an empty
list makes `leastAdapters.SelectPod` believe the pod carries the fewest adapters
and schedule onto it. A nil `*PodArray` from `ListPodsByModel` passes the
`podsArr == nil` guard in gateway_req_body.go:302 (a typed nil inside a
`types.PodList` interface is not `== nil`), then `CountRoutablePods(nil) == 0`
turns a model that does have pods into a 503 `no ready pod available`.

### Why CI did not catch it

- `test/integration/` is where the informer and the controllers actually run
  concurrently, and those ginkgo suites do not run with `-race`.
- `make test-race-condition` does cover `pkg/...`, but `pkg/utils/utils_test.go`
  carries `//go:build !race`, so the ginkgo suite of this package is excluded
  from race builds entirely (`go test -race ./pkg/utils/` reports
  `no tests to run`).
- The existing `Registry` unit tests are single-threaded, so the interleaving is
  never produced in the first place.

### Evidence

Running the controller integration suite under the race detector, on main:

```
KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS=<abs> go test -race -count=1 ./test/integration/controller/...

Ran 81 of 81 Specs in 179.400 seconds
SUCCESS! -- 81 Passed | 0 Failed
--- FAIL: TestAPIs (179.40s)
    testing.go:1490: race detected during execution of test
```

All 81 specs pass; only the detector fires. Six reports, all on this one cache,
writes at registry.go:92 and :95, reads at registry.go:110.

The race is also observable without the detector. With a writer that only
re-stores keys that already exist -- so the map holds exactly 8 entries for the
whole run, and there is no legitimate state with fewer -- 50,000 `Array()` calls
on main reliably return 1 to 2 **empty** snapshots. The `CustomizedRegistry`
equivalent returns a nil array about once per 300,000 reads.

## Changes

`values []V` + `valid bool` become a single `atomic.Pointer[[]V]` (nil meaning
invalid), and `CustomizedRegistry.values` becomes `atomic.Pointer[A]`:

- Readers do one `Load()`, so the pointer and the length always come from the
  same snapshot. The lock-free read path that #884 introduced is preserved.
- Writers publish by copy-on-write and never mutate a snapshot that has already
  been handed out. `updateArrayLocked` allocates the snapshot at exactly
  `len(registry)` capacity, so a caller cannot grow into it either.
- `CustomizedRegistry.Store`/`Delete` now invalidate *after* updating the
  embedded registry. Invalidating first lets a concurrent `Array()` publish a
  snapshot that misses the update and keep it permanently; invalidating last
  makes the worst case one wasted rebuild.
- `CustomizedRegistry.updateArrayLocked` returns the value it just built instead
  of re-reading the field. That re-read was the lost update behind the nil array.

The public API, the method signatures and the nil-receiver behaviour are
unchanged. No caller distinguishes a nil result from an empty one (checked
across `least_adapters`, `bin_pack`, `store_providers`, `cache_metrics`,
`cache_log` and `informers`), so publishing an empty snapshot for a fresh
registry is not observable.

The read path does not get slower. `Array()` + `Len()` in parallel, ns/op:

| values | before | after |
|--------|--------|-------|
| 8      | 3.7 - 5.9 | 4.3 - 4.7 |
| 64     | 4.6 - 7.1 | 4.0 - 5.5 |
| 256    | 7.2 - 8.5 | 4.4 - 5.6 |

One atomic pointer load replaces copying a three-word slice header plus a bool.

## Tests

Four cases added to the existing `Registry` suite in
`pkg/utils/registry_test.go`. Three of them fail on the current code:

```
[Fail] should keep the array returned by Array() unchanged after later updates
    Expected <[]string | len:2>: ["key3", "key2"]
    to consist of <[]string | len:2>: ["key1", "key2"]
[Fail] should keep Array() and Len() consistent while registry is updated concurrently
    Expected <int>: 6   to equal <int>: 0
[Fail] should keep the array returned by customized Array() unchanged after later updates
FAIL! -- 29 Passed | 3 Failed
```

After the change: `Ran 32 of 32 Specs ... SUCCESS! -- 32 Passed | 0 Failed`.

The fourth case (concurrent `CustomizedRegistry.Array()`) does not fail reliably
on the current code without `-race` -- the lost-update window is two adjacent
instructions wide -- so it is included as the analogue of the `Registry` case
rather than as a before/after proof.

Verified:

```
go build ./pkg/...                                                    clean
go vet ./pkg/utils/                                                   clean
go test -count=1 ./pkg/utils/...                                      ok
go test -race -count=1 ./pkg/utils/... ./pkg/cache/...                ok, 0 races
go test -race -count=1 ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...                      ok, 0 races
go test -race -count=1 ./pkg/...                                      0 races
KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS=<abs> go test -race ./test/integration/controller/...
                                                     ok  183.764s, 0 races
```

The integration suite reported six races before this change and none after.

## Related Issues

None; found by auditing `pkg/utils` and confirmed by running the controller
integration suite under `-race`.

---

## Follow-ups (deliberately not in this PR)

- Adding `-race` to the integration job would have caught this. Not touched here
  because `AGENTS.md` asks before changing `.github/` workflow policy.
- The `//go:build !race` tag on `pkg/utils/utils_test.go` hides this whole
  package's specs from race builds. Removing it currently surfaces unrelated
  pre-existing findings in the package, so it is left for a separate change.

title: [Misc] Add unit tests for pod key helpers and random pod selection
body:
## Pull Request Description

Adds unit tests for three previously untested functions in `pkg/utils/pod.go`. No production code is changed.

`GeneratePodKey`, `ParsePodKey` and `SelectRandomPod` were all at 0% statement coverage.

**`GeneratePodKey` / `ParsePodKey`** — covers the well formed key, the rejected shapes (more than two segments, no separator, empty input), and the three inputs that split into exactly two segments while leaving one of them empty (`"a/"`, `"/name"`, `"/"`).

Those last cases record the observed behaviour rather than assert that it is desirable, and a comment on the table says so. Every caller builds keys with `GeneratePodKey` from Kubernetes object fields, and the only three `ParsePodKey` call sites iterate `metaPods`, whose keys are inserted that way — so a key with an empty segment is not reachable through the current call graph. Writing `want: false` there would have meant changing production behaviour on a path no caller exercises.

A separate round trip test pins down that the two functions are inverses for well formed input.

**`SelectRandomPod`** — the injected `randomFn` makes selection deterministic, so the test asserts *which* pod comes back rather than merely that one does. Covers:

- the empty input and all-unroutable error paths, including that the returned pod is nil;
- the first, middle and last selectable index;
- a mixed list where `randomFn` must receive the count *after* `FilterRoutablePods`, not the length of the input — the test captures the argument `randomFn` is called with to check this.

Package statement coverage goes from 58.3% to 59.8%; all three functions reach 100%.

Verified that the new assertions actually constrain the implementation, by mutating the production code and confirming the expected tests fail:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `GeneratePodKey` separator `/` → `-` | 6 subtests fail |
| `ParsePodKey` `len(parts) != 2` → `< 2` | only `three_segments_are_rejected` fails |
| `ParsePodKey` returns `parts[1], parts[0]` | 6 subtests fail |
| `SelectRandomPod` drops `FilterRoutablePods` | 2 subtests fail |
| `SelectRandomPod` passes `len(pods)` to `randomFn` | only the mixed-list subtest fails |
| `SelectRandomPod` ignores `randomFn`, returns index 0 | 4 subtests fail |

`gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` and the full package test suite pass locally.

N/A — no tracking issue. Continues chipping away at the coverage gap, in line with the 90% total-coverage goal noted in `.github/workflows/lint-and-tests.yml`.

title: [Misc] Add unit tests for SLOQueue rank path and SLO branch precedence
body:
## Pull Request Description

Follow-up to #2718, where review noted that the specs covered `queueRank` (a path gated behind `queueOverallSLO = false`) but not the live `rank()` path that `Peek` actually calls, nor the SLO branch precedence in `rankImpl`. This PR closes that gap. No production code is changed.

**`rank()`** — three specs:

- zero elapsed time: `rank = expected − target` on a profile that meets the SLO (negative rank, no violation)
- elapsed term: passing `RequestTime + 2s` shifts the rank by exactly +2
- a profile with no SLOs propagates `errNoSLO`

**`rankImpl()` branch precedence** — the dispatch order `TPOT > TTFT > TPAT > E2E` ( slo_queue.go ) is pinned through the `target` value each branch computes. SLO values are chosen so every branch yields a *distinct* target (TPOT: `0.1×100+0.5 = 10.5`, TTFT: `0.5`, TPAT: `0.01×(2+100) = 1.02`, E2E: `9`), so the asserted number reveals which branch ran. Each spec drops one higher-priority SLO and asserts the target falls through to the next branch.

The TPAT spec calls `req.PromptLength()` rather than hardcoding the prompt token count, so a tokenizer change breaks the existing signature-pinning spec instead of silently corrupting this one.

Also asserts `expected` alongside `target` in the TPOT/TTFT specs, with profile tables filled with distinct values (E2E=1.0, TTFT=0.2) so a branch reading the wrong table fails.

Mutation check: swapping the TPOT and TTFT branches in `rankImpl` fails exactly the precedence spec and nothing else, confirming the assertions pin the dispatch order.

Coverage for the touched functions: `rank` 0%→100%, `rankImplTTFT` 0%→100%, `rankImplTPOT` 0%→83%, `rankImplTPAT` 0%→78%, `rankImpl` 62.5%→87.5%. The remaining statements are the "should not reach here" error paths on prompt/token length.

## Test plan


Both pass.

title: feat(gateway-plugin): add lockedRoutingStrategy to pin per-model routing strategy
body:
## Summary

Add `lockedRoutingStrategy` to the `model.aibrix.ai/config` annotation so admins can pin a routing strategy model-wide and prevent clients from overriding it via the `routing-strategy` request header.

### New resolution priority (highest → lowest)

1. `lockedRoutingStrategy` (top-level) — always wins when set
2. `routing-strategy` request header
3. `routingStrategy` from the resolved config profile
4. `ROUTING_ALGORITHM` environment variable

Behavior is unchanged when `lockedRoutingStrategy` is unset.

### Usage

```yaml
annotations:
  model.aibrix.ai/config: |
    {
      "lockedRoutingStrategy": "pd",
      "defaultProfile": "default",
      "profiles": {
        "default": { "routingStrategy": "pd" },
        "batch":   { "routingStrategy": "random", "requestsPerSecond": 50 }
      }
    }
```

Profile selection via `config-profile` stays alive — the lock only pins `routingStrategy`. The `batch` profile above can still tune `requestsPerSecond`; its `routingStrategy` is simply ignored while the lock is set.

### Use cases

- **Pin PD for disaggregated deployments** — a model served with separate prefill/decode pools must always go through `pd`. Clients sending `routing-strategy: random` can no longer break the prefill/decode split.
- **Per-model strategy on mixed clusters** — when a cluster mixes PD and non-PD models, each model pins its own strategy via its own annotation, independently of the global `ROUTING_ALGORITHM`.
- **Predictable routing for SLO/audit** — latency-sensitive models can be locked to `slo` / `least-latency` / `prefix-cache` so routing stays auditable.

## Changes

- `pkg/plugins/gateway/configprofiles/configprofiles.go`: add `LockedRoutingStrategy` to `ModelConfigProfiles`; split `ResolveProfile` into `ResolveConfig` (returns profile + locked strategy) and keep `ResolveProfileFromPod` for callers that only need the profile.
- `pkg/types/router_context.go`: add `LockedRoutingStrategy` to `ResolvedConfigProfile`.
- `pkg/plugins/gateway/util.go`: propagate the locked strategy in `applyConfigProfile`; check it first in `deriveRoutingStrategyFromContext`.
- Tests: unit tests for `ResolveConfig` and `deriveRoutingStrategyFromContext`, plus four integration tests covering lock-wins-over-header, lock-without-resolvable-profile, invalid-lock-returns-400, and a regression check that the header still wins when no lock is set.
- Docs: `gateway-plugins.rst` (field reference, priority table, example) and `pd-disaggregation.rst` (how to pin `pd`).

## Non-goals / Limitations

- **Backend compatibility is not validated.** The lock bypasses the per-request override, so the admin must ensure the pinned strategy matches the deployment: `pd` requires disaggregated prefill/decode pools; cache-aware strategies depend on the engine exposing prefix-cache state. Forcing an unsupported strategy will fail or degrade routing.
- **An invalid `lockedRoutingStrategy` returns 400 for every request** rather than silently falling back. This is intentional (fail loud over silently routing somewhere unintended), but a typo in the annotation makes the model unavailable until corrected.
- **Models without the annotation are unaffected.** Existing deployments need no migration.
- **`pd_disaggregation.go` keeps using `ResolveProfileFromPod`** (not `ResolveConfig`) because PD routing-config resolution happens inside the algorithm, after the locked strategy has already been enforced upstream in `deriveRoutingStrategyFromContext`.

title: feat(bot): add explicit Area field to Issue Forms, use as primary source
body:
## What

Adds an explicit **Area** dropdown to all three Issue Forms (bug report,
feature request, RFC) and makes `classify_issue()` use it as the primary
source for the `area/*` label, falling back to the existing keyword regex
matching only when it's absent or set to "Not sure".

## Why

Closes part of #2714: "Issue labeling can still assign unrelated `area/*`
labels because the bot matches broad keywords across the entire Issue
body." For example, a bug report describing a runtime issue that also
happens to mention "CI failures" and a "helm upgrade" in passing currently
gets `area/runtime`, `area/cicd`, **and** `area/installation` all at once.

This implements two of #2714's proposed-direction bullets:
- Add an explicit Area field to Issue Forms.
- Use keyword matching only as a fallback for Issues.

I scoped this PR to the Issue-labeling half only. The PR-side of #2714
(area labels from changed file paths) is already handled by #2711's
path-based labeler (merged). The remaining bullets - default `kind/*`
labels baked into the forms themselves, an Area section on the PR
template, and reconciling labels from older bot versions - are
independent of this change and are better left for separate, smaller
follow-ups rather than one large PR.

## How

- `AREA_FORM_OPTIONS` maps each dropdown option to its existing
  `area/*` label (no new labels introduced), keyed by the same
  `_clean_heading()` normalizer already used for Issue Form section
  parsing, so punctuation in the option text (e.g. "CI/CD") doesn't
  need to match the submitted answer exactly.
- `classify_issue()` reads the Area section from the parsed body; if it
  resolves to a known option, that's the *only* area label applied. If
  not (no Issue Form, field left as "Not sure", or an issue filed
  before this change), behavior is 100% unchanged from today.
- This is purely additive - no existing classification changes unless a
  submitter opts into picking an area.

## Testing

Extended `--self-test` with two new cases and ran it locally:

```
$ python3 .github/scripts/aibrix-bot.py --self-test
AIBrix bot self-test passed
```

1. A bug report with an explicit `Area: Runtime` selection, whose body

2. The same body with `Area: Not sure` - asserts the original
   multi-label keyword-matching output is preserved unchanged
   (`area/runtime`, `area/cicd`, `area/installation`), confirming the
   fallback path has no regression.

Pure Python stdlib + GitHub Actions YAML, no OS-specific code - runs the
same on Linux/Mac/Windows and in CI (`ubuntu-latest`).

title: [Bug] Guard SLOQueue.queueRank against zero throughput
body:
## What this PR does

`SLOQueue.queueRank` divided by the throughput read from the GPU profile without checking for zero, and `SLOQueue` had no unit tests at all. This adds the guard and the first specs for the function.

## The defect

`ModelGPUProfile.ThroughputRPS` returns an error only when the whole `Tputs` table is absent. A zero cell *inside* the table is returned as a valid `0.0`, so `queueRank` computed `float64(sub.Len()-1) / 0` and returned `NaN` when the sub-queue held only the head request, or `+Inf` when requests were queued behind it — in both cases alongside a nil error, leaving `Peek` with no signal to skip the profile.

That matters because `Peek` orders profiles with `q.higherRank(...) < 0`. Every comparison involving `NaN` is false, which leaves `sort.Slice` with an inconsistent less function, and `Inf - Inf` is `NaN` too, so two zero-throughput heads would hit the same problem.

This is reachable with the project's own data: `simulator-llama2-7b-a100.json` has zero entries in `tputs`, including the whole top output-length row, which `GetSignature` clamps any longer request onto.

## The fix

`PendingLoadProvider.GetConsumption` already performs the same division and already guards it with `ErrorSLOFailureRequest`, and `Peek` already skips a profile when `queueRank` returns an error. This applies the established pattern rather than inventing one — two lines:

```go
} else if throughput == 0.0 {
	return 0.0, cache.ErrorSLOFailureRequest
}
```

## Tests

Three specs, on a hand-built `ModelGPUProfile`:

1. The test request maps onto the intended cell — pins the fixture, so a change to `GetSignature` or the index layout fails here rather than confusing the specs below.
2. A zero-throughput cell returns `ErrorSLOFailureRequest` and a zero rank.
3. A non-zero-throughput profile with two queued requests returns a finite rank, verifying the `(len-1)/throughput` arithmetic on the success path.

Spec 3 passes the head request's own `RequestTime` as `currentTime`, so the elapsed term is exactly zero and the assertion does not depend on wall-clock timing.

## Note on scope

The original PR was test-only and characterised the NaN and `+Inf` values instead of fixing them. Following review, it now fixes the defect, since the path is gated behind `queueOverallSLO` (a package-level `bool` fixed at `false`) and carries no user-facing risk, and since the codebase already had the guard elsewhere.

## Test plan

```
go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/ -run TestQueue -v
golangci-lint run ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/...
```

Both pass.

title: feat: [API] Add per-replica inflight and RPS limits to config profiles
body:
## Pull Request Description Adds two config-profile fields so a model can cap load **per replica**, not only as a cluster-wide RPS total: - `requestsInflight`: per-pod concurrent-request cap. Saturated replicas are filtered out before scoring; if every replica is at the cap (or the chosen target is still full), the gateway returns **429** (`replica_inflight_exceeded`). - `requestsPerSecondPerReplica`: per-replica RPS. The gateway multiplies it by the current routable replica count and enforces that as the existing model RPS limit, so throughput scales with replica count. Takes precedence over `requestsPerSecond` when both are set. Values below 1 are expressed as “1 request every N seconds” (window capped at 1 hour). Either field forces routing to **least-request** so the per-replica figure actually holds. Redis-backed running-request counts (per-pod hash keyed by gateway instance, with heartbeat liveness so a crashed gateway’s contribution is excluded/pruned) drive inflight admission and several routers (`least_request`, `prefix_cache`, `pd_disaggregation`, `load_balance`). If Redis is unavailable, those reads fall back to the local atomic counter. Also refunds a rejected model-RPS increment immediately, and uses `ExpireNX` so refunds cannot stretch the rate-limit window. Includes unit, integration, and e2e coverage, plus the mock `replica-limits.yaml` profile.
